Eighty-one minutes into a game that meant far more to Samaleswari Sporting than the scoreline could explain, Veer Arjun Joshi stood over a free-kick with the scores level at 2-2. He was 19, a debutant in Kolkata and a long way from the academies in Spain and England where much of his football education had taken place.
The wall belonged to Mohammedan Sporting, one of Asia's oldest football clubs. Joshi bent the ball over it and into the net. Samaleswari won 3-2, and somewhere in that arc lay much of what the 135th IndianOil Durand Cup has offered its youngest players.
A Stage Measured in Moments
For a young footballer, opportunity rarely announces itself. It arrives as a moment, and what matters is what the player does with it.
At this year’s Durand Cup, 11 young footballers have made those moments count. They arrived by different routes, representing teams from different corners of the country. Some were shaped by the discipline of Armed Forces football, others by regional leagues away from the game’s usual spotlight, and a few by clubs building structured development pathways.
What connects them is the platform the Durand Cup provided to compete, learn and be noticed. The Durand Football Tournament Society extended that by recognising two Emerging Players from Groups A, B, C, E and F, and one from Group D, with each receiving Rs 1 lakh.
Group A had Md. Altab Hussain and Rinshid V of South United FC; Group B had Saikhom Borish Singh of Indian Army FT and Joshi of Samaleswari Sporting; Group C had Samuel K. Vanlalpeka and Naorem Somananda Singh of Indian Air Force FT; Midul Doley of FC Raengdai was the Group D pick; Kyrmenskhem Mukhim of Langsning FC and Dawancha Carlos Challam of Nongkseh SS & CC were selected from Group E; while Rituraj Mohan of Bodoland FC and Lalpekhlua Lalpekhlua of Karbi Anglong Morning Star FC completed the list from Group F.
The Air Force Believers
For Somananda of the Indian Air Force Football Team, the tournament has doubled as a classroom. His defining moment came against Defenders FC, the Sri Lankan Armed Forces side, when the ball broke loose outside the box and he met it with a strike that flew into the net.
It was his first goal against international opposition and, by his own reckoning, the high point of his career so far.
“The goal I scored against the Sri Lankan team, Defenders FC, was the biggest moment of my career, I think,” he said.
The goal was only part of the experience. Sharing a pitch with established professionals allowed him to study details that training alone cannot replicate.
“We study their body movements, their positioning, and exactly how they react when they lose the ball,” he said.
That, for Somananda, is what the Durand Cup offers beyond its history: direct exposure to teams operating at the top end of Indian football.
“We play against superior teams which play in the ISL, like Jamshedpur, and professional teams like Delhi. They are very professional teams. We learn a lot from them,” he said.
ALSO READ | East Bengal’s road to Durand Cup semifinals: 14 goals, one goal conceded and a transformed defence
He is already looking at where that experience could lead.
“It’s a very prestigious tournament and one of the best platforms for upcoming players. As an emerging player, I would say it’s an incredible stage to perform and showcase our talents so that we can improve, get noticed, and eventually make it to the national team.”
His Air Force teammate Samuel K. Vanlalpeka shares that ambition. His standout moment came against SC Delhi, one of the bigger sides in the competition, when he found the net.
“For me, it was the match against SC Delhi. They are a big team. We showed that we can perform against a big team and that we have the right attitude. For me personally, scoring that goal was also a special moment,” he said.
Playing established professionals and foreign footballers offered lessons beyond the result.
“There has been a lot to learn and a lot to improve from this experience. Playing against big players, big teams and good foreign players gives you a lot of experience. It helps you physically and mentally. It will definitely help me improve and drive me forward.”
For both players, the tournament has provided something difficult to recreate elsewhere: a direct measure of where they stand and how much further they must go.
Joshi and the Common Language
Joshi’s moment against Mohammedan Sporting carried similar weight for player and club. Samaleswari arrived in Kolkata as debutants from Sambalpur, Odisha, while his own journey had taken him from the United States through academies in Spain and England.
He did not take the chance lightly.
“I’m just thankful that Samaleswari Sporting has given me the opportunity to play,” he said.
His journey has also shaped how he views the diversity within Indian football, where players arrive from different regions and backgrounds before finding a shared vocabulary on the pitch.
“It doesn’t matter where you’re from, what language you speak or how you were brought up. Football becomes the common language,” he said.
The other Emerging Players demonstrate just how wide that common ground can be.
South United’s Structured Climb
At South United FC, the paths taken by Altab Hussain and Rinshid show why a structured pathway can matter.
Altab, a 19-year-old striker from Manipur, had already made his name in Bengaluru’s Super Division and earned two India Under-20 call-ups before spending three years within South United’s programme.
At the Durand Cup, he carried that experience onto a bigger stage, with his direct running and willingness to attack making him one of the club’s brighter performers.
“I feel very grateful to win the Emerging Player Award. It is a special moment for me and a great reward for the hard work I have put in,” he said.
ALSO READ | SC Delhi’s road to Durand Cup semifinals: 21 goals and an attacking storm
The tournament also gave him a clearer understanding of what remains ahead.
“I learned a lot about how to play against top teams and handle difficult situations on the pitch. It showed me the level I need to reach and what I need to improve,” he said.
“My goals are to play for the Indian team and the ISL one day. I know there is a lot of work ahead, so I want to keep improving every day.”
Rinshid’s story followed a different path. The 20-year-old central midfielder from Malappuram, Kerala, had never been part of a structured football setup until South United scouts spotted him during regional trials.
Two years with the club gave him the training he had previously lacked, and the Durand Cup offered his first chance to test those foundations against stronger opposition.
“It was a great experience playing against some of the best teams in the country. Playing at this level gave me the opportunity to challenge myself and learn a lot,” he said.
His favourite memories came from facing bigger opponents and being recognised for how he performed against them.
“My favourite moments were playing against big players and winning the Man of the Match award. Those experiences gave me a lot of confidence.”
More importantly, the tournament changed how he saw his own level.
“Playing against big teams taught me that I can compete at a higher level. Now, when I play against other teams, I feel more confident and comfortable.”
The Emerging Player recognition added to that belief.
“Winning this award at this age makes me feel really proud. It gives me confidence and motivates me to keep working hard and improving,” he said.
“My next goal is to keep working hard and hopefully play in the ISL. I want to continue improving and get closer to that goal.”
Voices From Every Corner
Elsewhere, the other Emerging Players wrote their own versions of the same story.
Saikhom Borish Singh gave the Indian Army Football Team an energetic and direct presence in the attacking third, willing to take on opponents and create chances while adding goals of his own.
In Group D, Midul Doley was the sole Emerging Player selected, providing FC Raengdai with an attacking outlet during the club’s first Durand Cup campaign.
Shillong produced two more names whose attacking instincts stood out. Mukhim was a constant threat for Langsning FC, finishing the group stage with two goals and a willingness to drive forward whenever space opened up.
Dawancha Carlos Challam operated from midfield for Nongkseh SS & CC and finished with two goals and an assist, reflecting his influence further up the pitch.
In Group F, Rituraj Mohan brought work rate and defensive discipline to Bodoland FC while still providing a threat going forward, while Lalpekhlua gave Karbi Anglong Morning Star FC an outlet from the flank.
No two of the 11 followed identical routes. Some were shaped by Services football, others by regional leagues and academies away from the traditional centres of the Indian game.
ALSO READ | Indian football great Arumainayagam conferred Arjuna Award (Lifetime) 2025
Altab progressed through a structured club programme after making his mark in Bengaluru. Rinshid was discovered at a trial without a formal footballing background. Joshi’s journey crossed three continents before bringing him to a free-kick in Kolkata.
The Durand Cup placed all of them in the same arena as ISL and I-League clubs, foreign teams and seasoned professionals.
Somananda put the opportunity simply.
“We are very lucky. We got a very prestigious moment to participate in such a beautiful tournament. It is one of the oldest in Asia and India’s biggest tournament.”
The Society’s Bigger Picture
The Emerging Player recognition has also given the tournament a mechanism to look beyond its biggest teams.
Spreading the awards across all six groups meant performances from regional and debutant clubs could be acknowledged alongside those produced within established footballing structures.
That distinction matters because Indian football’s talent does not emerge from one place. It comes from Services teams, clubs in the Northeast, academies developing their own pathways and regional trials where a player can suddenly come into view.
For much of Indian football, discovery has often happened informally: a scout in the stands, a recommendation or a performance at the right moment.
The Emerging Player award gives that process some structure. Performances are recognised, players receive a financial reward and, perhaps most importantly at this stage of their careers, they are told that somebody was watching.
It does not make the tournament administrators the centre of the story. The players remain that. But for a competition with more than a century of history, creating a mechanism to identify its next generation adds another purpose to the stage it already provides.
What the Recognition Means
For Altab, the recognition carries a straightforward lesson.
“This award shows me that hard work really does pay off. It motivates me to work even harder and keep improving as a player.”
For Rinshid, it has arrived at a formative stage and strengthened his confidence. For Somananda, it reinforces his international ambitions. For Vanlalpeka, it is another reason to continue testing himself against stronger opposition.
For all 11, the message beneath the prize money is similar: their performances did not go unseen.
For Joshi, the moment was a free-kick against Mohammedan Sporting. For Somananda, it was a strike against international opposition and an education in what higher-level players do differently. For Vanlalpeka, a goal against SC Delhi helped strengthen the belief that he could compete against bigger teams.
For Altab, the award validated years spent within a structured programme and kept the ISL and national team within sight. For Rinshid, the tournament provided evidence that a player who entered structured football late could still hold his own at a higher level.
Borish Singh, Doley, Mukhim, Dawancha, Rituraj and Lalpekhlua had their moments too, each finding a way to stand out in a competition where opportunities for unfamiliar names can otherwise disappear quickly.
The Rs 1 lakh prize gives those performances an added reward. The more important part begins afterwards: the next match, the next trial and the next level up.
The 135th IndianOil Durand Cup gave these 11 players a stage on which to begin that climb. What they do with it will determine how the rest of their stories are written.

Nigeria date removed from South African pop star Tyla's world tour after boycott petition
- Published
Just days after South African singer Tyla released the dates for her upcoming world tour, Nigeria has been removed from the list of destinations.
On Monday, the Grammy winner announced details of her globetrotting appearances coming on the heels of the release of her second album A*POP.
Her official website initially named 34 cities, including Lagos, Johannesburg and Cape Town, where she would be performing, but by Friday, an updated list was published without the Nigerian city.
No reason has been given for the change but there have been growing calls in Nigeria for the 24-year-old to cancel her concert in the country over the recent wave of anti-migrant sentiment in South Africa.
Relations between Nigeria and South Africa have soured over allegations that Nigerians have been the target of xenophobic violence.
Nigeria, along with other African countries, has accused South Africa of not doing enough to deal with attacks on foreign nationals.
There have also been a series of protests with people calling for all undocumented migrants to leave South Africa. Tens of thousands of foreigners have left the country, including Nigerians, many of whom boarded specially chartered repatriation flights.
- Singer Tyla's racial identity sparks heated culture war 
  - Published9 December 2023
While there have been diplomatic efforts to calm tensions, most recently with a meeting between their foreign affairs officials in Abuja, the issue has spread beyond politics.
On Wednesday, an online petition titled "Ban Tyla from entering Nigeria until xenophobic attacks stop in South Africa" was launched in Nigeria and it has already attracted thousands of signatures.
On Tyla's social media pages, where the initial tour dates still appear, Nigerians cautioned her against performing in the country as they criticised her for failing to speak out against the protests in South Africa.
Tyla has so far not responded to a BBC request for comment.
Tyla is not the only South African artist facing a backlash for their seeming silence on the anti-migrant protests.
Comedian Trevor Noah also came under fire following an advert he fronted for the Tourism Business Council of South Africa.
The promotional clip, shared across the council's various social media accounts, generated many comments criticising the former Daily Show host for promoting South Africa but failing to call out xenophobic attitudes.
Users even went as far as to add context under the video saying South Africa was "a xenophobic country [that] doesn't allow visiting migrants".
The backlash has extended beyond criticism; some South African artists have reportedly lost out on performances across the continent.
South Africa's Justice Minister Mmamoloko Kubayi said in June that a local artist had told her that "all her gigs were cancelled". The minister did not name the artist.
"So the [South Africa] brand does get affected," she said at the time.
The South African government has also pushed back on the growing wave of criticism.
It says that it does deal with anyone who takes the law into their own hands, pointing out that more than 900 people were arrested after recent protests, but that it has a right to control migration into the country.
The online debate around Tyla's world tour has opened a much wider conversation on whether African artists be held responsible for the political tensions between their countries.
Nigerian activist, opposition politician and former presidential candidate Omoyele Sowore said on X that anger over anti-migrant attacks should be directed at political leaders in Nigeria and South Africa, rather than artists.
In a post, he said: "No-one should hold a talented musician like Tyla vicariously liable for the crimes of xenophobia. Artistes are not responsible for the failures of politicians except where there is ample evidence they're enablers."
Nigerian culture journalist Mayowa Idowu told the BBC that while the anger may come from a desire for accountability, directing it towards an artist risks missing the wider issue.
"I think they are well intentioned because people are seeking accountability and they're looking beyond governments who they do not trust or have faith in. That said, I think they are misguided and they risk devolving into acts of hypocrisy. The artist in question has worked with Nigerian artists and performed in Nigeria previously," he said.
Idowu argues that performers should not be pressured into taking political positions simply because of their nationality.
Tyla has found herself at the centre of rivalry between the two countries before.
Earlier this year, she beat four other African artists, including three from Nigeria, to clinch her second Grammy award in the Best African Music Performance category.
She won the inaugural version of the prize in 2024, again beating a field that included Nigerian heavyweights such as Burna Boy and Davido.
With two wins in the category's first three years, Tyla has become one of the biggest Grammy success stories in African music - while also becoming a symbol in a fan rivalry that often frames Nigerian and South African artists against each other.
UK-based Nigerian culture journalist and writer Dami Ajayi said that Tyla has never presented herself to be anti-Nigeria but "we interpret her winning two Grammy Awards in a nominations list full of Nigerian musicians as being anti-Nigerian".
"These targeted retaliatory campaigns are not particularly new. There were also calls to boycott the recent hit Netflix show The Polygamist, adapted from Zimbabwean Sue Nyathi's novel and co-directed by Akin Omotosho, a Nigerian living in South Africa," he added.
South African journalist Thango Ntwasa said that while it was difficult to comment on the removal of Lagos from Tyla's world tour line-up, "it's a very interesting time because we're seeing arts and politics... really confronting each other now more than ever".
He also touched on the criticism levelled at artists like Tyla and Noah on their apparent silence on the migration issue, saying that while it's understandable for artists to want to be apolitical, it was important for "celebrities... to understand that as a public figure, your opinion or position on a political issue does matter".
Ntwasa noted that South African artists had reported facing animosity when visiting other African nations and that, because touring is a big part of how they make money, the negative attitudes could affect them down the line.

Ayra Starr on her secret relationship and teasing Stevie Wonder
- Published
There's resilience, and then there's Ayra Starr.
Two weeks before the release of her new album, Starrgirl, the Nigerian singer posted a photo from hospital, after undergoing "major surgery".
"I was hoping it would be a quick recovery, but it was more complicated than they expected," she told fans, external, without disclosing the nature of the procedure.
Within seven days, she was back in the dance studio, rehearsing for forthcoming performances with a large bandage strapped across her stomach. TV appearances, fan events and live performances followed.
"I'm healing," she told the US breakfast TV show, Today. "I have strength today. I'm so happy I was able to even be here today and be able to do this."
It's a display of the tenacity and ambition that's defined Starr's career to date.
Discovered singing covers on YouTube at the age of 18, she became the first African woman to win best international act at the Mobo Awards, and the first Nigerian woman to surpass one billion video views on YouTube.
In 2024, she was the first Afrobeats artist to play Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage – and finished her set by declaring she'd return as a headliner. Last year, she modelled for Di Petsa at London Fashion Week, closing their show in a white lace two-piece, flanked by an angel.
So it's hardly a surprise that Starr pitches up to our interview with a sort of celestial confidence. She's given to grand proclamations like "I'm unstoppable", or "I will exist in multitudes". But somehow, she never sounds arrogant or conceited.
That's probably due to a sense of humour so dry it could soak up a tsunami. Starr is criminally sarcastic, and delights in winding people up.
For example: When music legend Stevie Wonder phoned to congratulate Starr on a Grammy nomination, she goaded him into a playful argument about zodiac signs.
"I was trying to one-up him every single time, and he was trying to one-up me. It was almost like a battle," she recalls.
Starr eventually got to the point where she told Wonder, a Taurus, that "Tauruses ain't crap".
"I'm sure he was like, 'Who is this? What do you want from me?' But it was a very cute conversation. I respect it."
It's an unorthodox approach to making friends, but it seems to work.
Over the course of her career, Starr's hooked up with Coldplay, Tyla, David Guetta, Le Sserafim and Kelly Rowland from Destiny's Child.
Her new album boasts collaborations with Afrobeats legends Wizkid and Rema, as well as One Direction's Zayn Malik and rising R&B singer KWN.
The album is her first under a new management deal with Jay-Z's Roc Nation, and a relocation to New York. Leaving Lagos was a big upheaval, she confessed in an essay posted to her Substack last year., external
"New York is basically a walk-in freezer with rent," she wrote. "It's so cold it feels like the city is actively trying to unalive my motivation… I'm not scared, I promise."
Secret relationship
Behind the move was a desire to explore new influences and expand her sound. So you get a track like Where Do We Go, which marries a sashaying Afrobeats rhythm to a hypnotic electronic pulse.
"Like, the rebel I am, I love to juxtapose," she says.
"I don't like being normal and boring. So the idea of writing a heartbreak song on a beat like that, where you can dance to it, was just very enticing. I love things like that."
The lyrics were inspired by a secretive relationship "that was stuck in a rut but I kept coming back to it".
We've all been there. It's all too easy to settle for an imperfect partner because they're a comfortable and familiar presence.
Starr admits the thought of starting over with someone else filled her with fear.
"You're back to square one, and somebody's asking for your favourite colour again.
"I'm like, 'Oh my God! Can we, like, not do that?'"
The problem with staying in the relationship, however, was the way it affected the rest of her life.
"You keep accepting things lower than your standard, and that influences every single thing in your life - because when you let yourself go, romantically and emotionally, it affects you physically, and the music, and all of that.
"So even though I enjoyed [the romance] while it lasted, I picked my priorities and what was most important to me. And that relationship wasn't as important as the music... or anything else."
The story could act as a metaphor for the entire album. After the runaway success of her breakout single, Rush, and her second album, The Year I Turned 21, Starr was beginning to feel trapped by other people's expectations.
"Just like any other pop artist, passive listeners get attached to the songs they know - the popular songs.
"Then you're stuck between creating for the passive listeners and creating for your core fans who want you to do more.
"So that can limit you, because you stop thinking as an artist and start thinking about making music just for consumers.
"But I'm not meant to conform. It's just not who I am. I will rebel against every single preconception and every stereotype."
So she's ditched the teenage angst of her debut, but also the poise of its follow-up. This is an album about walking to her own rhythm, as Starr grows into autonomy and womanhood.
On Misunderstood, she laughs at the people who told her she'd "never make it on her own"; while the laid back groove of Treasure allows Starr to pause and savour her success.
"Give me some fun / Pure enjoyment / Take a photo of me," she sings in Yoruba.
The most infectious song on the album is Ms Paper, which takes a detour into Bouyon – a Dominican music characterised by high tempos and frantic percussion. It was recorded almost by accident at the end of a session with French-Congolese star Theodora on a hot and sticky February night in LA.
They'd actually finished working for the day, and had just polished off a boozy dinner of Congolese food when inspiration struck.
"The AC in the studio wasn't working, so everybody's delirious, everybody's sweating, everybody's drunk," Starr says.
"At one point we're probably taking off tops. I changed outfit twice because I was drenched in sweat."
It sounds like a recipe for disaster, but when you play it back, you can practically see the steam rising from your speakers.
Live snippets of the song have already gone viral, suggesting Starr has another hefty hit on her hands. At the same time, she's faced criticism in Nigeria from people who feel she's diluting her musical heritage by chasing a more global sound
"People have a certain template they think I should follow, and it's like, you cannot tell me how to dream," she says.
"I'm able to honour my culture, but also try new things, because that's who I am."
Starr answers her critics, in a roundabout way, on her album cover - where she pairs a club-ready gold dress with a traditional gele headwrap.
"I wanted young girls in Kwara State or Erin-Ile to see this and feel represented," she told Capital Xtra, external.
"I'm not the first to do it, I won't be the last to do it - but I want people to feel confident in their culture and wear [the gele] like the crown that it is."
Not for the first time, her instincts proved right. Starr's stunning, retro-futuristic look has gone viral, inspiring dozens of copycats, and tempering at least some of the criticism of her new direction.
As she says in her new song, Amazing: "If they're gonna talk, I'll give them something to talk about".
"That's definitely my mantra," she says.
"And do you know what? I think I need to listen to myself more because I have all the answers in my music."

Four months after Karnataka became the first State to frame guidelines allowing multi-pair kidney paired exchange transplants, the initiative is yet to result in a single such transplant, with only one request having reached the State Authorisation Committee so far. August 13 is observed as World Organ Donation Day.
The request, involving a multi-pair swap arrangement for patients with incompatible donors, was approved by the committee but the transplant did not materialise following a misunderstanding between the donor-recipient families.
M. Shivalingaiah, chairman of the State Authorisation Committee, who heads the State-run Institute of Nephro-Urology, told The Hindu that the guidelines were framed and notified in April to provide an avenue for patients who had willing but medically incompatible donors.
“Before the guidelines were framed, we were receiving requests from patients who had willing donors but could not proceed with transplantation because of incompatibility. The idea behind the guidelines was to provide a structured mechanism for such patients to benefit from paired exchange,” he said.
Under kidney paired exchange, a donor who is medically incompatible with their intended recipient can donate to another compatible recipient, while the second donor gives a kidney to the first recipient. A multi-pair exchange extends this arrangement to three or more donor-recipient pairs.
One request approved, but swap fell through
Dr. Shivalingaiah said the single application received by the committee was approved after scrutiny, but the arrangement could not proceed because of a misunderstanding between the families involved. This involved patients enrolled with two private hospitals in Bengaluru and one in Hubballi.
“The framework is available, but people have to understand the process and come forward. The benefit cannot reach patients unless the donor-recipient pairs are willing to cooperate and proceed together,” he said.
The State notified the guidelines on April 4, operationalising provisions under the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act (THOTA), 1994, for exchanges involving three or more donor-recipient pairs.
The guidelines were framed in response to the difficulty faced by patients with incompatible donors, including those with ABO blood group mismatch, positive crossmatch or HLA incompatibility.
Strict safeguards
The framework permits multi-pair swaps only when each donor is a near relative of the intended recipient and the medical incompatibility of each pair is documented. Compatibility across the swap group has to be established through cross-match and HLA reports from the NABL-accredited laboratories.
All donors and recipients have to enter into a single joint agreement, and every case requires prior approval of the State-Level Authorisation Committee.. The committee is also required to interview each donor and recipient, with the proceedings video-recorded..
The guidelines prohibit any commercial transaction and require the clinical, immunological, psychological and legal evaluations prescribed under the transplant law to be completed before approval.
Where multiple hospitals are involved, the institutions have to submit an inter-hospital coordination plan, while the transplant procedures are to be performed simultaneously, as far as possible, to prevent the arrangement from breaking down.
Greater awareness
Dr. Shivalingaiah said greater awareness among potential donor-recipient pairs was necessary to make the framework work. “People should understand the opportunity available to them, come forward and make use of it,” he said.
“We had expected that the guidelines will provide an additional avenue for patients who otherwise face difficulty accessing a kidney transplant because of donor incompatibility. However, it is unfortunate that even after four months, such multi-pair swap transplants are yet to materialise in Karnataka,” he added.

OAS warns Haiti needs help as it prepares to hold elections for the first time since 2016
The secretary general of the Organization of American States says that Haiti needs help fighting gangs and seizing back territory as it prepares to hold general elections for the first time in more than a decade
PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti -- Albert Ramdin, secretary general of the Organization of American States, said Wednesday during a trip to Haiti that the country needs help fighting gangs and seizing back territory as it prepares to hold general elections for the first time in more than a decade.
Ramdin spoke as he concluded a trip to the troubled Caribbean country, where he met with the prime minister and other officials.
He said the new U.N.-backed gang suppression force needs more personnel, equipment and funding.
“The efforts of the (force) are essential to improving security and public safety, and to creating the conditions for a safe electoral process,” he said. “Progress must be visible and measurable as soon as possible.”
Ramdin said priorities are securing the main route to the main international airport; ensuring ongoing access to the airport and seaport; and restoring safe access to Haiti’s southern region. Gangs currently control the main routes leading in and out of the capital.
He also called on Haiti to step up registration and identification of voters ahead of the Dec. 13 general elections. Haiti hasn’t had a president since Jovenel Moïse was killed at his private residence in July 2021. Since then, gang violence has only surged, displacing a record 1.5 million people.
Ramdin promised to keep “mobilizing political, technical and financial support” for the Caribbean country.
He said the OAS will work with the Pan American Health Organization to build trauma centers to treat wounded Haitian police officers as they continue to push back against gangs that control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince and swaths of land beyond the capital.
Ramdin said he also plans to set up a delegation of business leaders to talk about potential investment projects in Haiti, where poverty, hunger and unemployment are deepening.
“Haiti is at a decisive point,” he said. “The future of Haiti belongs first and foremost to the Haitian people. But the international community also has responsibilities.”

Premier League predictions 2026-27: BBC Sport pundits pick their top four
- Published
Arsenal ended a 22-year wait to be Premier League champions last season, but can they successfully defend their crown?
That is the next target for Gunners boss Mikel Arteta, whose side finished seven points clear of nearest rivals Manchester City last time out.
So, who will challenge them in 2026-27? We asked 26 BBC TV and radio pundits to pick their top four, with explanations for their selections.
We've also asked AI's opinion, and included what Opta's 'supercomputer' came up with too.
The AI prediction was generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to "predict the Premier League table for the 2026-27 season".
Opta's 'supercomputer' is actually a complex algorithm that uses a model based on betting market odds and the sports analytics company's own 'power rankings', which are calculated using past results.
It has simulated the outcome of all 380 Premier League games 10,000 times and came to the same conclusion as AI, and three of the pundits.
Disagree with our expert humans or think you know more than any machine? You can make your own top-four prediction, and forecast the rest of the Premier League table, at the bottom of this page.
These predictions were made on the basis of how each squad shaped up on Thursday, 20 August, with 13 days to go until the transfer window shuts at 23:00 BST on Tuesday, 1 September.
Last season, only four teams featured in the forecasted top-four positions, but this time there are seven named, in 15 different combinations.
Overall expected ranking, using all 28 predictions is:
- Arsenal (109 points)
- Manchester City (73)
- Liverpool (38)
- Chelsea (35)
- Manchester United (21)
- Aston Villa and Tottenham (both two)
Calculated using a system of four points for a first place, three points for second, two points for third and one point for fourth.
Arsenal - 'Arteta's army marches on'
Last year, only 17% of BBC predictors (6/35) thought they would be champions. This year, 89% (25/28) think they will successfully defend their crown and no-one thinks they will finish lower than second.
Theo Walcott: They have got the biggest advantage of all - continuity. Mikel Arteta is still there, they are coming off an 85-point title-winning season and they have strengthened rather than rebuilt.
The Bruno Guimaraes signing is massive, to add to a midfield that already boasts Declan Rice and Martin Zubimendi. Their defence was also ridiculously good last season, although William Saliba's progress after his World Cup injury is something to watch closely.
Thomas Hitzlsperger: Arsenal are the team to beat. Unlike a lot of their rivals, they kept their manager and, every season, the team plays together and gets additions.
I still don't expect Arsenal to play nice football in the sense that I am excited to watch them play. I just think they really know what it takes to win, and they are going to do the same again this season.
Danny Murphy: It is always hard to call it now, especially when it feels like all the top teams have a lot of business to do before the transfer window shuts, but I can't look past Arsenal as champions.
The main reasons being the momentum and confidence they will have from winning the Premier League already, but also the consistency of having the same manager and same players and just sprinkling even more quality on top.
They have not lost any of their best players and they have got a group who know what the manager expects from them and are completely on board with it. Arteta didn't need to spend half the pre-season drilling them with his methods like a new manager has to.
Joe Hart: It's really important how Arsenal handle the scrutiny of being champions, but they will totally understand that and what is coming their way.
Leon Osman: They look like a team that are ready to have a run at winning three titles in the next four or five years.
Teams like United in the early Premier League days, Arsenal under Arsene Wenger and Jose Mourinho's Chelsea give me the vibes this team does. And the way they've strengthened brilliantly states the league isn't their only objective this season.
Matt Upson: They are my favourites again but I don't see them running away with it. Staying at the top is always harder - ask any manager - and you also have to remember there were spells when they looked like they had run out of steam last season and were grinding out results a lot of the time.
The biggest challenge for Arteta this year will be picking the right team, or rather resting the right players, for the right games and keeping players engaged and ready to step in when needed.
Chris Sutton: He will have to try to keep everyone happy but if you are fighting on all fronts, that's possible. They do look like they are at a different level, squad-wise.
They won the title in a bit of a different way so it will be interesting to see how they go about it this time, but it does look on the face of it like they can beat you up, or just play through you.
Nedum Onuoha: Watching them against City [in the Community Shield], you knew how they were going to play and so did their players. Arsenal have not just spent pre-season getting ready for this, they have spent the past five or six years building.
Glenn Murray: They have had continuity for several seasons now, plus winning the league has given the group a wave of belief that will see them win another title.
Michael Brown: It's theirs to lose. Arsenal should win the league because of the transition at other clubs, but also because of the quality and rhythm they have already got.
Rachel Brown-Finnis: Great squad depth and additions this summer. Arteta's army marches on!
Troy Deeney: They are the best team and they going to win the league by a comfortable margin. My only question is can they win the Champions League too? I still think they need an extra player in on that left-hand side to get that done.
Sue Smith: The way Bruno played in the Community Shield, it felt like he's fitted in already. There are probably still players that they will look to bring in, but they have got a couple of great options in every position now.
Ellen White: Bruno gives them something different again because he is so tenacious, an absolute warrior. Their midfield is formidable now, with Rice, Bruno, and Martin Odegaard to go in there, and then you have got Miles Lewis-Skelly too, almost saying "I'm still here" after the talk of him leaving. It's a great problem for Arteta to have.
I don't know if they will get another number nine this summer or not, but I still think they have more potential to be champions than any other team.
Tony Pulis: They are already strong enough defensively and they can score goals from everywhere. If they get the centre-forward they are looking for, they are going to be better than they were last year.
Shay Given: They might miss out on the title unless they sign a top striker in the next couple of weeks to help with the goal situation.
Paul Robinson: If Victor Osimhen comes in from Galatasaray, and they get Villa defender Ezri Konsa too, then it's a different conversation. But they are not the only team still trying to get deals done.
Man City - 'They are rebuilding but will still be up there'
City were the BBC predictors' pre-season favourites in eight out of their 10 seasons under Pep Guardiola from 2016 onwards, and were champions six times during that period. But before their first campaign with Enzo Maresca in charge, only 12% (3/26) think they will reclaim the title.
Thomas Hitzlsperger: City are the only English club to have been ever-present in the Champions League since 2011, which is an achievement in itself when you think about how competitive the top of the Premier League is.
With Pep Guardiola, I would always say they would finish in the top four, but now he has gone, and it is always so tough to follow someone like that. Maybe this is the year that City finally drop out.
Shay Given: I don't think Pep leaving means we will see what happened when Sir Alex Ferguson left United. Instead, I am expecting the opposite, because of a fresh voice in the dressing room. These players have not won the Premier League in two years so they will be hungry for success. City will be number one.
Troy Deeney: My prediction for City is not based off what happened in the Community Shield, it is based off what I saw with Enzo Maresca at Leicester and Chelsea.
I am not sure he has got that ability to really demand what he wants. Pep has taught all these coaches, but only Arteta has tweaked it and kind of said "I am going to use all the principles, but this is my way of doing it".
I don't want to be disrespectful, but Maresca is a BTEC version of Pep Guardiola. He plays a certain way and has no other way of dealing with it. You saw on Sunday how bad City were defensively but all of his teams are wide open, and he is still doing that now, even with better players - top-class players.
Joe Hart: City were clunky against Arsenal in Cardiff but I don't think they will over-react to one poor game. I think they still believe they've got the team and the quality to challenge.
Theo Walcott: Maresca replacing Pep is obviously a gigantic question mark, but City's squad is still absurd. The problem is the transition from Pep to Maresca, plus losing Rodri and others.
Nedum Onuoha: City have still got a bunch of players who have won the title before, but they have got a new manager and have also lost some of their more senior players.
Anita Asante: Maresca's playing style is not that dissimilar to Pep's so there is not this massive change in terms of the team's identity. They have still got some fantastic forward players too, but Rodri leaving is massive because we know how pivotal he has been at the club.
It's the same with losing John Stones and Bernardo Silva too. They were leaders in the dressing room and they will be missed there, as well as on the pitch.
Leon Osman: That signals problems for me, even with Erling Haaland there.
Pat Nevin: Midfield, management, you name it - City are rebuilding. I will be surprised if they win it, but they will still be up there.
Rachel Brown-Finnis: They still have some big guns, but will be too inconsistent to win the league.
Matt Upson: Even if Maresca struggles a bit at first, you look at the quality and experience in their squad and the goals in their team, and they still have enough to stay up there. I can't leave them out. City had that huge drop-off under Pep in the season before last, when they were terrible for a few months, and they still made the top four.
Danny Murphy: I look at the firepower City have got and, whoever the manager is and whoever they are playing against, they are still going to be able to score a lot of goals and win a lot of games. I would still have them as being Arsenal's nearest rivals.
Chris Waddle: The City midfield of Kevin de Bruyne, Rodri, Bernardo Silva and Ilkay Gundogan that won so much has all gone now, and they are replacing them with people where the expectation is they will grow into that City shirt.
They are trying to build a new team, and it might take them a year or two. They will still be in the top four, but the question is how well - and how quickly - they gel together.
Steph Houghton: Arsenal will be tough to beat but I still think City will push them, as soon as their players get back into a bit of form and find some rhythm.
This is the next era for City, with a new manager and new players, and I think the likes of Elliot Anderson will come good. Then there is Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki, plus Haaland of course. It's still a world-class squad.
Sue Smith: They are going to add to their midfield so it's hard to predict what they will do until the end of the transfer window and we know who they've got, but Anderson will be a success there.
There is a lot of pressure and expectation on his shoulders but he is a brilliant player and it just seems like he'll be able to cope with that.
Ellen White: City want Enzo Fernandez from Chelsea, but I am not sure he is the right player for them. And, whoever comes in, it is going to take time to find the right balance in midfield.
Chris Sutton: There's no doubt the pressure will be on Maresca from the off, and replacing Rodri is nigh on impossible. They are in for Lille's Ayyoub Bouaddi, who is a talented player but he is 18, and would be a massive gamble.
Michael Brown: City are in transition, and a lot depends on who they bring in. But if they have a really impressive end to the window, it changes everything.
Liverpool - 'A work in progress but Iraola is exciting'
Last season, 22 of 35 BBC predictors had them down as champions and only three thought they would finish lower than second. This time, only four of 28 have them finishing higher than third.
Danny Murphy: Liverpool might need a bit more time before they are challenging for the title again. I am also not sure whether they think they have already got enough to replace Mohamed Salah by bringing in Victor Munoz and maybe giving Rio Ngumoha a bigger role, or whether they are really going to go for Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola, or someone like him, in the next few days.
Michael Brown: They look light to me as I write this. Who are they going to get to improve them?
Lindsay Johnson: Liverpool and Chelsea are in the same boat because both new managers will take time to settle in, and Liverpool probably don't have a big enough squad to last a full season playing the football Andoni Iraola plays.
Theo Walcott: Liverpool are probably the hardest team to call. Iraola is an excellent manager and if Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz have big seasons, they could absolutely push Arsenal for the title.
Thomas Hitzlsperger: I've gone for them to finish second because I really like the way Iraola's teams play. Also, I am kind of biased here because I am really hoping Wirtz has the season now that people expected him to have last year.
Paul Robinson: Wirtz looked a different player towards the end of last season and they also have a manager who has proved himself, and is Premier League ready.
Sue Smith: I know it's a completely different level and expectation managing Liverpool and it's going be interesting to see how he does in that sort of step up, but all you can judge Iraola on is what he's done at Bournemouth and I think he's been brilliant. Defensively is my concern, though. Especially the right-hand side.
Anita Asante: It will take time for Liverpool to adapt to Iraola's style, which is closer to Jurgen Klopp's. I am excited, because that means high-tempo, high pressing and playing on the front foot, but that's why it's even more important they sign reinforcements to strengthen their defence.
Glenn Murray: They have got all the forward players you could dream of, but Iraola has a big headache when it comes to finding the right balance between attack and defence.
Troy Deeney: They are decently balanced although I still think they need an additional left-back and an extra midfielder. Ultimately they have got one X-factor - Isak. He is a top goalscorer who has got a point to prove because everyone has written him off.
Rachel Brown-Finnis: Iraola is Liverpool's most exciting signing in recent years. Liverpool's football DNA will be back.
Leon Osman: Liverpool are a work in progress. Older players leaving, new managers in. Some good signings at the back but will Iraola get them firing straight away? I'm not sure.
Chelsea - 'They are potentially going to be unplayable'
Last season, Chelsea figured in all 35 top-four predictions, and finished 10th. This time, they are in 21/28 predictions, with five people backing them to be runners-up.
Pat Nevin: As usual my top four is only a guess but it's the triumvirate of Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers up front that makes me back Chelsea to be in there more than anything else. They are a group who are exciting, and brilliant as well. It will be fascinating to see how they get on.
Sue Smith: They have been using Palmer and Rogers as two number 10s in pre-season, which is frightening. They are potentially going to be unplayable.
Michael Brown: They have got all this talent but as usual it is still about them finding the right balance. They might surprise people and be solid.
Joe Hart: Their squad is well built, and they don't have European football.
Nedum Onuoha: It's a ridiculous anomaly for teams like Chelsea or Spurs to not be in Europe, and being able to focus on domestic football while they have both been spending such big money.
Matt Upson: There seems to have been a big change in their transfer policy and the balance of their squad looks a lot better for them to be able to win trophies.
Troy Deeney: No Europe means more time on the training pitch, so Xabi Alonso will be in a great position to figure out what works best. I wouldn't be surprised if they finished second, because I can't split them, City or Liverpool.
Glenn Murray: Alonso is coming in with a point to prove after what happened at Real Madrid, and he has made some shrewd signings, including some experienced players who can help their young team-mates harness their enormous potential.
Chris Waddle: Having Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson in the team will be like having a coach on the pitch. Yes they are 35 and 36 now, but I played in the Premier League until I was 36 and I didn't really find it hard. You still have your brain and, even if your legs have gone a bit, you can have legs around you.
Step Houghton: That experience is what people were saying they were missing last season.
Tony Pulis: I really rate Alonso and bringing in Welbeck and Henderson was almost an act of genius because if, you look from the outside, the problems at that club are because there has been no-one in the dressing room to pull up the young players when that has been needed.
Thomas Hitzlsperger: Chelsea are probably the team I am most optimistic about when I look at the manager.
Anita Asante: Alonso will give them structure and bring an identity to the team but he won't restrict the players. I feel like he will give them the freedom to express themselves.
Theo Walcott: Alonso gives them the stability they have been missing. If Palmer stays fit, I can see them being one of the most consistent teams outside the title race.
Man Utd - 'The mood at the club feels different'
Last season, none of the BBC predictors backed United to make the top four, and they finished third. This time they figure in 14/28 predictions, although only one of them has them improving on last year's position.
Thomas Hitzlsperger: United can stabilise themselves this season.
Michael Brown: The legs of the squad is still a concern, and the Champions League could make them unstable.
Anita Asante: The mood at the club just feels different, compared to how dysfunctional they were under Ruben Amorim or Erik ten Hag.
Ellen White: Unlike last season, Carrick has got Champions League football to contend with. I like Youri Tielemans as a signing, but they need more in... and is Marcus Rashford staying?
Paul Robinson: The best thing Carrick can do with Rashford is put his arm around him and try to get the best out of him. It's difficult enough anyway to find another player at his level, but especially when you have already got him and don't have to pay anything for him.
Steph Houghton: Rashford staying would be a massive bonus because we know his quality and he has a different skillset to a lot of the forwards they have already.
Chris Waddle: They have Rashford back at the moment but is his heart in it? Or his head? I think he's had a taste of being abroad and I'd be surprised if he doesn't want to try it again.
Matthew Upson: In the time Carrick was there, from January onwards, United showed they are definitely top-four material, and they are the ones I found it hardest to leave out.
Tony Pulis: I still don't think United, over a season, will do it with what they have got at the moment. They might still get three or four in, and that changes the picture but, right now, they are short. Arsenal and City are miles ahead of them.
Troy Deeney: I've got United down as fifth. A solid year, but nothing special. I don't think they have got a great squad so they will be out of the Champions League by February and then they can concentrate on the league.
Lindsay Johnson: United's defence needs work but they may sneak in fourth.
Anyone else? - 'Villa are so good under Emery' and 'can you ever trust Spurs?'
Lindsay Johnson: I've put Villa in there again because of Unai Emery and his experience.
Leon Osman: Villa have been brilliant the past few seasons but they keep letting their best players go. How long can Emery keep over-performing with what he's given?
Thomas Hitzlsperger: Villa being in the Champions League means they are probably going to be in the top six rather than the top four, but they are just so good under Emery.
Glenn Murray: Tottenham are going to be much better than last season. They have made some great signings and James Maddison is back fit. My only worry for them is that they still need a goalscorer.
Leon Osman: Their signings, plus injury returns should see Tottenham competing where they expect to - but can you ever trust Spurs?
Paul Robinson: Spurs had a shocker last season but this time they are on the fringes of the Champions League places, without a doubt. When Roberto de Zerbi took over last season, he wanted guarantees in the transfer market this summer - and judging by the players he has brought in, he got them.
Newcastle are miles off it, though. I cover the Saudi Pro League and Matthias Jaissle is a good coach who plays attractive football - but he needs the players and at the moment they don't have them.
Troy Deeney: After finishing 17th two seasons in a row, expecting Spurs to be in the top five is a big ask. It is Nottingham Forest who are my surprise package this year - I know people will say they have lost Anderson but, the way they play, I don't think he is a massive loss. The owner is ambitious and so is Oliver Glasner, so it is a marriage made in heaven.
Nedum Onuoha: I am going with Leeds and Sunderland to surprise people. A few people are expecting Sunderland to struggle because they are in Europe but the owners are a bit more ambitious than people realise. They won't necessarily be fifth in November, but I don't think they will be down the bottom either.
The same for Leeds. Staying up last year was huge, and now they are thinking about part two of who they want to be, and part two features things like signing a goalkeeper for £40m.
Steph Houghton: Sunderland are playing more games this season and have not been able to boost their squad yet, but hopefully that will happen next week. But they were seventh last time and will be there or thereabouts again, especially if they can sustain their home form.
Tony Pulis: I don't see Villa making it although they are a good side. I don't think any of the teams like Bournemouth, Brighton and Brentford - who were all in the top 10 last season - will be anywhere near the relegation places, but it is very difficult for them to get into the top four.

They have spent quite a lot, and brought in about a dozen players, like Sunderland did last year, and again they have brought in a similar type of player too, with a lot of athleticism.
Their manager Gary O'Neil did all right at Wolves and Bournemouth and he will be as well-equipped as ever to know which games to go after, and when to dig in.

Deadly attacks on aid workers and contractors surge in South Sudan as UN urges protection
At least 36 humanitarian workers and contractors have been killed in South Sudan since January, surpassing last year's total of 31
JUBA, South Sudan -- At least 36 humanitarian workers and contractors have been killed in South Sudan since January, surpassing the 31 killed in all of 2025, as violence persists in the country that's one of the most dangerous for aid workers, the U.N. humanitarian coordinator there said Wednesday.
“These are not just statistics,” Ramanathan Balakrishnan said in a statement marking World Humanitarian Day, adding: “Every killing must be investigated, and those responsible held accountable. The continued loss of humanitarian personnel, overwhelmingly South Sudanese nationals, is unacceptable."
More than 450 incidents of violence against humanitarian workers and assets were reported between January and July, more than double the number recorded during the same period last year, according to the U.N. Mission in South Sudan.
Renewed fighting between government forces and opposition fighters has forced aid organizations to relocate from some areas, further restricting access to vulnerable communities in a country of about 12 million people that has struggled with both conflict and the effects of climate change since independence from Sudan in 2011.
Humanitarian organizations are calling on the South Sudan government and all parties to the 2018 peace agreement meant to end civil war to protect aid workers, investigate attacks and ensure safe and unhindered access to people in need.
Around 10 million people are expected to need humanitarian assistance this year, including more than 7.5 million facing high levels of acute food insecurity, according to the U.N.
Last week, the U.N. refugee agency and World Food Program warned that more than 650,000 refugees and asylum seekers in South Sudan risk losing access to lifesaving food, nutrition and other assistance because of severe funding shortages.

The Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has transferred the processing of pending citizenship applications under the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), 2019, from Empowered Committees —comprising Central government officials, including those from the Census, Intelligence Bureau (IB) and postal departments— to district Collectors in eight States and Union Territories (UTs).
District Collectors in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, West Bengal, Assam (except tribal areas), Tripura (except tribal areas), Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh have been authorised to process CAA applications, as per the August 19 order, making the earlier arrangement of multi-agency committee redundant.
The order is significant as the amendments to the CAA Rules, which first came into effect on March 11, 2024, have been notified after the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) came to power in West Bengal. The amendments brought in days before 2024 general elections had concentrated the powers to process the citizenship applications of members of six non-Muslim communities from Pakistan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh, who entered India before December 31, 2014 without any documents or illegally.
The CAA was strongly opposed by the then Trinamool Congress (TMC) government in West Bengal. To bypass the role of the State government in processing the applications, MHA constituted at least four Empowered Committees —two at the district level, headed by Central government officials— to clear the citizenship applications. The committees were created days before the Assembly polls in West Bengal in April this year.
A large number of the Matua community, comprising Hindu Namasudras with roots in Bangladesh, and an important electoral block are the intended beneficiaries of the CAA in West Bengal. Though the legislation was brought in for undocumented migrants, the Rules mentioned several documents to be provided by the applicants including a document issued by a government authority in Pakistan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh following which several Matuas could not find their names in the voter list after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.
Citizenship is a subject under the Union List of the Constitution and State’s role could have come in play in providing logistics such as office space and police verification of applicants.
Citizenship Amendment Act: Legal issues and status of judicial proceedings | Explained
What the August 19 order states
The order issued by the MHA on August 19 states that all applications pending before the Empowered Committees and District Level Committees in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, West Bengal, Assam (except tribal areas), Tripura (except tribal areas), Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh will be transferred to the concerned Collector.
The order also makes the March 11, 2024 MHA notification implementing the Citizenship Amendment Rules inapplicable to these jurisdictions. Two subsequent MHA orders issued in February and March 2026 have also been rescinded, while actions already taken under them have been protected.
The Citizenship (Third Amendment) Rules, 2026 notified on August 19 empowers Collectors in these jurisdictions to receive, scrutinise and dispose of applications for registration or naturalisation under Section 6B of Citizenship Act.
Under the amended rules, the Collector is required to verify the documents submitted by an applicant, conduct any necessary enquiry, administer the Oath of Allegiance and determine whether the applicant meets the eligibility requirements. If satisfied that the applicant is a fit and proper person, the Collector can grant Indian citizenship.
An application can be rejected if the applicant fails to appear personally to subscribe to the application and take the oath despite being given reasonable opportunities.

Former Fauci adviser Dr. David Morens pleads guilty to concealing COVID-related records
Dr. David Morens, a former senior adviser to Dr. Anthony Fauci during the COVID-19 pandemic, pleaded guilty in federal court Tuesday to a charge of conspiracy to defraud the United States.
Morens, who worked under Fauci at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, was accused of concealing federal records related to coronavirus research. He was indicted in April for allegedly trying to hide email exchanges about that research by using his personal email instead of his government email.
"By pleading guilty today, Dr. Morens has taken responsibility for what he did, and he will continue to do so," his legal counsel, Tim Belevetz, told NPR in an email Tuesday.
Morens has apologized in previous hearings for his handling of federal records.
The coronavirus research in question has come under fire by Sen. Rand Paul and other Republicans, who have claimed without proof that the coronavirus that caused the pandemic came from a lab in China, and have accused Fauci and Morens of covering that up. Both scientists have denied this. Many researchers agree that the weight of the available evidence suggests the virus emerged naturally.
Fauci, who played a leading role in the United States' pandemic response, was not charged with anything in connection with Morens. But earlier this month, Paul's Senate committee voted to hold him in contempt of Congress for invoking the Fifth Amendment against self-incrimination and refusing to answer questions at a hearing. It will ultimately be up to the Justice Department to decide whether to pursue a criminal prosecution of Fauci.
Some experts have said these moves are part of broader undermining of science and scientists in the United States.
Jennifer Jones, who runs the Center for Science and Democracy at the Union of Concerned Scientists, would not comment specifically about either Morens' or Fauci's situations. But she says the Trump administration has been attacking scientists in many ways.
"Criminal prosecution of scientists is a classic authoritarian tactic," she told NPR in an interview.
But Robert Fisher, a Boston attorney who is not involved in the Morens case, says the government's charges against Morens appear solid.
"When you're a government official you swear an oath, you're working for a federal agency, you're just held to a higher standard," Fisher said.
Morens, who is 78 years old, could face five years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 when he is sentenced in November.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leaders hoisting the party flag instead of the Tricolour on 15 August 2026 in Chhattisgarh. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows BJP leaders hoisting the party flag instead of the Tricolour on 15 August 2026 in Chhattisgarh.
Fact: The video is from a BJP training programme held in Kurud, Chhattisgarh, on 22 March 2026, where the BJP flag was hoisted before the programme. Bhanu Chandrakar, BJP Programme In-charge in Kurud, clarified that the video was being shared as Independence Day footage and said that a police complaint was filed. Kurud MLA Ajay Chandrakar also clarified that the video was from the March training programme and condemned its circulation. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google keyword search to check whether BJP leaders hoisted the party flag instead of the Tricolour on 15 August 2026 in Chhattisgarh. However, we found no credible reports confirming the claim.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to the same video (archived) uploaded on the Instagram account of Bhanu Chandrakar, a BJP worker and BJP Programme In-charge in Kurud, on 23 March 2026. This confirms that the viral video predates the 80th Independence Day on 15 August 2026 and is unrelated to the event. According to the post, the video shows the inauguration of the Pandit Deendayal Upadhyaya Training Maha Abhiyan in Kurud, Chhattisgarh. The training programme was scheduled for 22 and 23 March 2026 and began with the hoisting of the BJP flag in the presence of guests, office-bearers and party workers.
Upon reviewing Bhanu Chandrakar’s Instagram account, we found a clarification post (archived) dated 15 August 2026. Chandrakar stated that the video was being falsely shared as footage of BJP leaders hoisting the party flag instead of the Tricolour on Independence Day. He said the content was being circulated by some news channels and Congress social media pages and added that he, along with BJP Kurud office-bearers, had approached Kurud Police Station and filed a complaint seeking action under cybercrime laws.
We also found a video (archived) posted by Bhanu Chandrakar on 15 August 2026, showing the Independence Day celebrations in Kurud. The post states that Municipality President Jyoti Bhanu Chandrakar hoisted the Tricolour at the Kurud Municipality office and later at the main ceremony held at Mangal Bhavan.
Kurud MLA Ajay Chandrakar also posted a video clarification (archived), stating that the viral video was from a BJP training programme held on 22 March 2026 and was falsely presented as footage from Independence Day. He condemned the claim and said that the BJP’s Dhamtari district unit had filed a complaint against those responsible for sharing it.
To sum up, an old BJP training video was shared showing BJP leaders hoisting the party flag instead of the Tricolour on the 80th Independence Day in Chhattisgarh.

Beebom Score
Game Freak has spent decades teaching us how to catch monsters, train them, and throw them into chaotic battles. So, seeing the studio walk into the action RPG world with Beast of Reincarnation felt a little like watching Growlithe take on monsters in an open arena to me.
Beast of Reincarnation is an ambitious action RPG set in a post-apocalyptic Japan in 4026, where Emma and her blighted canine companion, Koo, travel through the world swallowed by nature. Well, the mix of sword combat, parrying, skill trees, and Koo’s turn-based attacks is surely distinct from any other Game Freak titles.
While those systems can take some time to get used to, the result is a genuinely fascinating game hidden underneath a few rough edges that hooked me far more than I anticipated. So, here’s my Beast of Reincarnation review where I talk about the standout features alongside the areas where it fell short.
The First Hour Nearly Made Me Regret Starting Beast of Reincarnation
I’ll admit that Beast of Reincarnation initially had me worried. Setting aside the lower-tier fodder enemies, the first boss fight against the Rangifer made me feel like I accidentally signed up for another Souls-like exam. Defeating the hybrid Nushi was certainly a steep wall at first, but not in the “controller throwing” way I remember from my first few hours with Sekiro.
Thankfully, the parry system in Beast of Reincarnation is remarkably forgiving, offering generous timing windows. After a few encounters, I stopped treating every incoming attack like an impending nuclear strike and actually started leaning into the rhythm of battle.
To my extent, none of the bosses in this game approach the sheer personal hostility of Gyoubu Oniwa or Sword Saint Isshin of Sekiro, let alone the enemies of some of the popular souls-like games. In my opinion, the learning curve is far more approachable for any beginner RPG gamer.
Parries, Powers, and Perfect Timing Make Combat Surprisingly Addictive
The clever part of the combat in Beast of Reincarnation is how Emma and Koo complement one another. Attacking and successfully parrying enemies can help build the resources required to unleash Emma’s stronger abilities and feed into Koo’s special attacks.
Suddenly, combat doesn’t feel like just swinging a sword until something stops moving. It’s more like I’m watching the enemy, waiting for an attack, landing a parry, building my meter, and deciding whether it’s time to unleash Koo. The mix of real-time action and command-based inputs is easily one of the game’s best ideas.
However, if parrying isn’t your entire personality, there are ranged weapons and other abilities to fall back on. Weapons like the Spring Thunder Crossbow and the Zangetsu Bow can become an absolute powerhouse with the right upgrades.
Koo and Emma Make One Heck of a Team
Koo is undeniably the star of Beast of Reincarnation. Yes, he’s an adorable dog and shows more emotions than Emma, but more importantly, he is immensely useful in combat.
This is where Game Freak’s classic DNA shines through. Giving commands to Koo feels strangely familiar, except now, my “Pokémon” is a massive dog capable of helping me dismantle the massive nightmarish creatures.
Koo’s attacks aren’t just flashy animations. With enough Fluorescence Points collected by successful parries, I can decide when to call on him strategically into a battle. His moves produce satisfying attack combinations with Emma, giving the combat a two-character rhythm. Moreover, it never felt like taking control of Emma away from me.
This makes a smart design choice that gives the game its distinct identity compared to other RPG titles that it draws inspiration from.
Then there’s Emma herself, whose hair is apparently far more versatile than anyone I know of. Her hair can function as a grappling tool, create temporary paths, and help her gain vertical height for air strikes and stealth assassinations.
A Gorgeous Post-Apocalyptic Japan That Begs to Be Explored
The world is one of the strongest selling points of Beast of Reincarnation. This isn’t the usual gray, miserable apocalypse where everything looks like it has been dipped in concrete. Instead, nature has aggressively reclaimed the civilization, creating lush green landscapes with overgrowth on buildings.
There are resources, upgrade materials, food ingredients, Cleanse Walker parts to collect, along with a bunch of goodies scattered around. However, I occasionally felt compelled to revisit an area, simply because I loved being there.
Eventually, I reached a point where I would rather follow the story than spend another ten minutes grinding and searching for the ingredients to make a meal that I wasn’t particularly desperate to cook. This isn’t because the exploration is bad; rather, the rewards rarely made me desperate to investigate every nook and corner.
The More I Played, the More Beast of Reincarnation Started Showing Its Cracks
While Emma’s emotional detachment is explained by the game’s story, I still struggled with the protagonist. The narrative no doubt has plenty of layers, yet Emma often feels like she’s just a passive observer rather than participating in her own journey. I kept thinking about how powerful certain moments could have been if she had shown more personal depth.
The gameplay momentum also hits a wall with boss recycling. The initial encounters were exciting because I was learning their attacks and figuring out when to parry. Then, the game started bringing some of those bosses back. Again, and again. The problem is that the individual fights aren’t terrible, but the repetition is what drained my enthusiasm.
A similar issue plagues the audio design. While the atmospheric soundtrack fits the mood initially, I realized that I was hearing the same style of music over and over again. For an action RPG focusing on discovery and mystery, a broader and more dynamic soundtrack would have gone a long way.
Performance: My RTX 4060 Had Little to Complain About
My experience was considerably better than some of the harsher PC reports that I’ve seen. I waited for the major Beast of Reincarnation update patch before properly playing, and I have never experienced the crashes or black-screen problems.
My Setup:
CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 7435HS
Motherboard: LA-N591P Laptop Motherboard
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060
RAM: (2x12GB) 4800MHz DDR5
SSD: M.2 PCIe Gen 4×4 NVMe SSD
I did encounter occasional stutters, but they were rare and roughly one in ten times in my experience. I also noticed some amusing collision problems in cramped spaces, where Koo would pass through Emma or decide to share the same physical space as his human companion.
Verdict: Beast of Reincarnation Has the Bones of Something Great
Beast of Reincarnation is a genuinely solid action RPG game. The combat system is clever, Koo is a standout companion, and Emma’s hair traversal adds fun mobility. The world boasts a unique visual identity that keeps me interested.
However, the recycled bosses, soundtrack repetition, and uneven visuals make the $60 price point a bit tough to justify. Beast of Reincarnation feels like Game Freak discovering a new playground and then forgetting to fill every corner of it.
With the combat clicks, I genuinely had a good time. Landing a perfect parry, building my resource, calling Koo into the fight, and following it with a powerful attack never got old. Traversing the world with Emma’s bizarre hair-based mobility also grew on me far more than I expected.

Five Australian rules footy players apologise amid police investigation

Five players in the Australian Football League (AFL) who were suspended for late-night drinking and inviting women to a hotel have publicly apologised to their club and fans.
The Sydney Swans' Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice have been stood down from Australian Rules football's top league for the rest of the season, the club announced earlier on Wednesday.
The suspension comes after Melbourne detectives began an investigation into an alleged sexual assault, said to have to taken place in the early hours of Monday at the Pullman Hotel where the players were staying after Sunday's match.
None of the players have been arrested or charged in the investigation.
"We are deeply sorry to everyone involved," the players said in a statement posted to the Sydney Swans website.
"We know we have let down our partners and families, members, supporters, teammates, the AFLW team, corporate partners and everyone at the Club and in the wider community.
"We accept the Club sanction and apologise for the impact this has had on those involved."
Sydney Swans chairman Andrew Pridham also apologised to fans, players and the wider community earlier on Wednesday.
Speaking to reporters, he explained that the sanctions were handed down because the players had breached the club's standards by drinking alcohol later than accepted and bringing women to the hotel.
In a statement announcing the suspensions, the club said: "We respect there is an ongoing investigation by Victoria Police and the actions we have taken today are independent of this.
"The AFL is supportive of the Club's sanctions."
Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich told a media conference: "We're deeply embarrassed and ashamed that the poor choices of five of our players, and the impact that's had on the women involved and also the club.
"We are deeply concerned about their welfare and the wellbeing of those women."
He declined to say whether any of the players had been drug tested, saying that any testing would form part of the police inquiry.
A spokesperson for Victoria Police said officers have spoken to several people who were at the Pullman Hotel, but no one was formally interviewed or arrested.
On Tuesday, club officials held talks with the players ahead of their suspension.
AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon has described the reports of the alleged sexual assault as "deeply concerning".
Sydney has dominated this season, currently placing second on the ladder which guarantees them a spot in the qualifying and elimination finals' round that begins in two weeks.
The club is scheduled to play against North Melbourne at the Sydney Cricket Ground on Sunday, which will be the last fixture ahead of the finals.
Heeney and Warner are considered two of the sport's biggest stars.
Unlike some other Australian sports, the AFL does not have a strict no-fault stand-down policy on players charged with serious offences such as sexual assault, and instead handles cases on a discretionary and case-by-case basis.
