California passes toughest wildfire rules in the U.S. for home landscaping
As severe wildfires burn across the Western U.S., California has adopted the toughest rules in the country to help protect communities from burning. Homeowners in wildfire-prone areas will be required to limit plants within five feet of their house, a protective measure that wildfire experts say can help prevent homes from igniting.
Research shows that dry, dense vegetation around buildings can cause wildfires to spread. In extreme conditions, high winds carry a deluge of tiny, burning embers far beyond the fire itself. When those embers get caught in vegetation, they can ignite, spreading flames to nearby buildings and homes.
Wednesday's vote by the California Board of Forestry and Fire Protection comes after years of debate and delays. The state originally considered rules that would have restricted all vegetation within five feet of a house, aside from well-maintained trees. That generated pushback from some communities, concerned about losing greenery in their gardens and the cost of yard maintenance.
California regulators ultimately struck a compromise about plants allowed within the five-foot zone, known as Zone Zero. Lawns, flowers and non-woody plants up to 18 inches tall will be allowed, unless they are located directly under the roofline of a house. Trees will be allowed, though branches must be trimmed five feet away from a structure. The rules will apply to new construction right away, but will be phased in for existing structures, affecting almost 2 million homes in high-risk areas.
State regulators say the rules reflect the new reality of more extreme wildfires, driven in part by rising temperatures from climate change. More than 57,000 homes and buildings have been destroyed in California in the last decade, according to state regulators.
"California's faced an existential crisis that has affected our health, that has affected our finances related to our ability to buy and sell homes, to insure homes and has put us in a very precarious place," testified Yana Valachovic of the University of California Cooperative Extension at Wednesday's hearing, who also advised the state on the new rules.
Growing tensions across Western states
California's debate reflects growing tensions across the Western U.S. about how communities should prepare for wildfires. Wildfire experts warn even fires that start in open, wildland areas can quickly become urban fires, destroying thousands of homes in neighborhoods that residents never thought were at risk, like in the 2025 Los Angeles fires. This summer, more than 800 homes were destroyed in Spokane, Wash., by three wildfires that burned through dense neighborhoods.
Across several states, homeowners in public meetings have said wildfire regulations threaten private property rights, reduce urban wildlife habitat and require costly maintenance.
"You are about to approve a set of regulations that will cost millions of California homeowners tens of billions of dollars," testified Dave Lefkowitz, president of the Mandeville Canyon Association, a community group in the Los Angeles hills. "The math is insuperable."
Vegetation management rules were recently defeated in both Oregon and Washington after strong public pushback, including misinformation that spread online. Some community groups wanted regulators to wait for more scientific research on wildfire spread.
Research shows plants can increase risk
In experiments, researchers have shown that even green plants can ignite in the dry, windy conditions of an extreme wildfire. Analyses of past California wildfires have also shown that homes with vegetation predominantly within six feet of the exterior walls were at higher risk of being lost. Managing vegetation also creates "defensible space" for firefighters, providing better access for defending a structure.
California has long been at the forefront of wildfire policy, pioneering regulations that other states have adopted. For almost 20 years, California's wildfire building codes have required homes to use fire-resistant materials for construction. A handful of other states recently adopted similar codes. Research shows that while there are no guarantees a house will survive a fire, protections are strongest when homeowners address both building materials and vegetation. Even in some of the most severe wildfires in recent years, some homes made it through.
California regulators say the widespread regulations are needed because voluntary measures don't provide enough protection. Communities are safest when all homeowners comply, since one home with dense, dry vegetation can spread fire to its neighbors. Insurance companies in California are also required to provide discounts to homeowners that make their homes more fire-resistant.
New rules depend on inspections
While California's new rules provide more flexibility for homeowners, some wildfire experts say they don't go far enough, given that any combustible material next to a house could pose a risk. The new vegetation rules will be enforced by local fire departments and state agencies that do home inspections every year. Those inspectors will bear the brunt of educating homeowners and ensuring compliance.
"I want the board to understand what this compromise asks of local inspection programs," Todd Lando of the Central Marin Fire Department testified at the hearing. "A clean Zone Zero is a five-minute inspection with one question: Is anything combustible within five feet? Easy for the homeowner to understand and take action on." Lando says the new rules will involve more conditional judgements by inspectors, opening up debate with homeowners that could affect compliance.
California regulators say inspectors will focus on educating homeowners at first, before compliance becomes mandatory. For existing homes, the new vegetation rules will go into effect in 2029 at the earliest.

The Trump Administration Wanted Her Expertise, Just Not Her
An interview with the transgender CIA analyst fired from Trump’s White House
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts
When Julia Curlee was a kid growing up in Hawaii, she dreamed of becoming an intelligence officer. In 2007, when she took her oath standing on the marble CIA seal, she achieved that goal. But she had another childhood dream too: She’d always had “an unshakable belief that I should have been born a woman.”
In 2013, Julia Curlee became the first CIA officer to transition openly and keep serving the agency. She felt more effective at her job living as the person she always believed she was—and years ago wrote about her experience under a pseudonym in The Atlantic. Her performance proved her effectiveness: She became the daily intelligence briefer for Vice President Pence during the first Trump administration and a director on the National Security Council in both the Biden administration and the second Trump term.
Less than 70 days after the president returned to office in 2025, Julia was fired from the White House without explanation. She returned to the CIA and, over time, began to feel a lack of support at the agency in an administration that was openly hostile to transgender people. Julia left her dream job with the federal government earlier this year. This week, she is telling her full story for the first time—in an Atlantic essay she wrote and in a conversation with Radio Atlantic.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Julia Curlee: After everything I had been through with my service to the former vice president, my briefing for this president in the first term, and my war zones, my 20 years, all of it, “Be discreet” meant We need you. We need your service. But we don’t want anyone to know you are here.
Adam Harris: As a high-level CIA officer, Julia Curlee had the ear of one of the most powerful politicians in America: the vice president of the United States. He relied on her to let him know what was going on in the world each day. She held prominent intelligence positions during the last three administrations: Trump 1, Biden, and Trump 2. She is also a transgender woman.
For a long time, Julia had two dreams: to be a CIA officer and to be her authentic self. She realized the first in 2007, when she took the oath on the agency seal; the second in 2013, when she transitioned.
She made a promise when she did: never to hide who she was. Yet in 2017, she wrote two stories for The Atlantic under a pseudonym. She wrote about her experience; she wrote about what it meant for the intelligence community to accept people like her. The agency used it to help recruit on college campuses. Julia was using the discretion that came naturally for a CIA officer.
Now, after being pushed out of the White House and leaving an agency where she no longer felt supported, Julia is telling the rest of the story as herself.
I’m Adam Harris. This is Radio Atlantic, and today: a conversation with Julia Curlee.
Let’s get to questions.
Julia, welcome to the show.
Julia Curlee: Thank you, Adam. Thanks for having me.
Harris: Absolutely. So Julia, you served the United States for more than 20 years in intelligence positions. What was it that drew you to public service?
Curlee: Well, I grew up a barefoot kid in Hawaii, and I always wanted to see what was over the horizon and see the world and all that. And then, at some young, impressionable age, I was ambushed by The Hunt for Red October and the analyst as hero, getting to save the day. And, I don’t know, it sort of came out of nowhere and it sort of bubbled up in my life. And my parents definitely instilled in me a desire to serve our country, and intelligence just caught something in me and I wanted to be a part of it.
Harris: When you joined, was it everything you imagined?
Curlee: Oh, many more late nights and long PowerPoint-presentation sessions.
Harris: So not quite like the movie?
Curlee: Not so much, yeah. I didn’t call in many drone strikes on my way to the PowerPoint presentation that you would sometimes see in the movies. Did not repel off a helicopter into a submarine too many times.
But it was an amazing and wonderful career. I got to travel to 35 countries. I briefed several presidents. It was just all I wanted to do, and I desperately wish I was doing that now. It’s the only thing I ever wanted to do and it was the only plan I ever had.
Harris: And today you’re writing in the pages of The Atlantic, telling your story for the first time under your own name. Why now?
Curlee: Well the institutions that I served through my adult life are under assault. The ability of officers to speak truth to power, to inform policy making so that they make the best decisions on behalf of the United States—that is being eviscerated. And the officers who deliver that, who spend their lives learning about foreign countries, learning how to systematically understand multiple sources of intelligence, convey uncertainty—all of that is being destroyed by an administration that wants to both cherry-pick the intelligence to only receive what they want to hear, and to punish the officers who have the courage to speak that truth to them, to do their jobs and to live up to the values that we inculcate in all of our officers. And so the only way to do that was to leave and to begin to tell my story.
I also felt like I needed to tell the other part of my story, which has nothing to do with my substantive experience in the world, and that’s being a trans person. And I know that the sustained assault on people like me is a part of a broader campaign to try to define who gets to be in public spaces, who gets to have positions of honor.
Harris: I want to talk about that service and about your transition while you were in the service. You transitioned in 2013, and did you have concerns when you were transitioning? What was that first day going into the office like?
Curlee: Well, it was the most terrifying day of my life. And that was in the wake of several war-zone assignments and being rocketed, and I didn’t know whether it would be the last day.
You know, as I already said, I’d always dreamed since I was a kid of being an intelligence officer. The other dream that I’d always had that was unexplainable was just an unshakable belief that I should have been more born a woman.
I didn’t know where it came from. It just was always lurking in the background. And over time in my life, it became this just unshakable darkness that clouded out everything else. And finally, I came to the conclusion I had to transition. The only problem, of course, is that there were no trans people. The last time someone at CIA had tried to transition had been decades before, and it had been terrible. The person had been driven out of the organization, in a hostile workplace, and management had not been supportive. And so I contacted the LGBT group to say, Hey, I’m here. I’m here to meet other people and get some help. And they said, Congratulations, but you’re the only one.
And that is what led me in 2017 to write in pseudonym in The Atlantic under the name Jenny Hall. And it was an opportunity to get the word out that people like me are a part of our national security, that we’re patriots, that we want to serve, that we don’t want any special rights. We just want what everyone else has.
And so I was very happy to get to do that. And in the years following that, CIA actually used those articles on college campuses to recruit people. And I was very proud of that, but I was also very, very happy to disappear back into my day job, in the work.
And so, you know, in short, my transition in those years was a big “nothing significant to report,” in the lexicon of my profession, and that was the best possible outcome.
Harris: So when you talk about the work, this is 2017; the first Trump administration has just begun. What were your concerns? Did you have concerns ahead of that first Trump administration about their policies, or the platform, regarding transgender people?
Curlee: You know, going into that term, it really hadn’t been in the political realm very much. I mean, it honestly wasn’t a big issue. It only really became, in my consciousness anyway, a big political issue when the president, the first time, banned trans people in the military, which was a shock, because for a lot of us it was a rock-solid belief that progress is linear, that things you gained might slow down, but, you know, the long arc, and that things would get better. And this was a case of it regressing in a significant way.
And I knew several trans intelligence officers who were in uniform who were doing the same job that I was doing at CIA, and they were being told that by being honest, by which the previous administration had told them they could be, that they would be thrown out and that their careers would be destroyed just for being themselves. And so I also wrote about that to try to make the case in a good-faith way to our leaders that this was the wrong decision and that it would hurt our national security.
Harris: So you gave the president’s daily brief during that first Trump administration. Can you tell us what it means to do that job and what all it entails?
Curlee: Yeah, so as a baby analyst, you imagine yourself being that briefer in the room with the commander in chief or briefing on Air Force One. It was the thing that most of us aspired to at the end of a long career. And initially I was assigned to the deputy national security adviser in the White House. And boy, it was like cramming for a final exam every morning from midnight to 5 a.m. or so. And then at some point there, you’re whisked downtown and you come to the White House when it’s pitch black and you check in with the Situation Room, and you’ve got these pieces that you’ve been studying. And so I would get to the White House and I would find my—I’d be the first person that would see my policy customer when they came in the door in the West Wing, the deputy national security adviser, at first, and I would be in there for 15, 20, 30, 40, 50 minutes, and it would be 20 questions, and it would be firing things at me and asking me to follow up with taskings. And it was just exhilarating for a person that was a news junkie who wants to be plugged into the information universe, just wanting to be available to help these policy makers make good decisions. And I did that for two years in total for the Trump administration for the first term.
Harris: And so, while you’re in the Trump administration, you begin giving the president’s daily briefing, and you begin giving that briefing to Vice President Mike Pence. What was the experience of first meeting him like?
Curlee: Yeah, so I’d been in the PDB for a few months, and it was wonderful. And as much as I loved roaming the West Wing of the White House before dawn and no one caring apparently that a trans woman was serving the highest levels of the Trump administration, my boss walked into my office one day and said, you know, Julia, what would you think about briefing the vice president? And I looked up at her and I said, This vice president?
And she said, Yeah, I think you’d be the right pick for this. And I took her word for it. And so, the first time I was standing in the driveway at the Naval Observatory when there he was, unmistakably, with his silver-white hair, and he turns to his outgoing briefer and said, You’re gonna abandon me with her? And it was his dad-joke humor, and there I was, and it was just me and Mike Pence.
And I discovered that he was an excellent intelligence customer. He took the book, he took the briefing almost every day, religiously. He took rapid notes and would be firing questions at me. And he really impressed me with how seriously he was taking the job of being this consumer of intelligence, this massive, multibillion-dollar apparatus we’ve built out to help our leaders make better decisions. And he was using it as I would have hoped he would. And in a broader administration where that was not always the case, I really felt like I could really do good, and support him as he participated in these policy conversations. And it was a real pleasure. It was truly the thing that I had been training and and wanting to do since I’d been a kid. It was like the experience that I dreamed of.
Harris: Yeah, so he was really relying on you for your expertise?
Curlee: Yeah, I mean, I would be one of the first people he would see in the morning. It has been described to me that a PDB briefer is—part of your job is, like, helping to filter the world so that a policy maker whose most precious commodity is time can know what are the really big issues to focus on. And I would play that part in his day, in focusing him on the key events happening in one part of the world versus another, teeing up information so that I would know what policy-making meetings he was going into or heading on a foreign trip, and I would be trying to anticipate his needs, and then when he asked a question, ensure that it was rapidly answered as quickly as possible. And so getting to travel with him around the world, getting to be a part of the team that follows the vice president, was truly an amazing privilege.
And for all of the fears and my own trepidations—I wasn’t ignorant of his public persona. It truly was a great experience, and I got to see our government operating as it should.
Harris: There’s probably some dissonance there, right, between that public persona and the private persona? How do you square the difference between the public policy and and the person who you engaged with on a regular basis?
Curlee: I don’t know, and I don’t want to suggest that I know his personal views. What I know is what I experienced. I experienced being treated with great respect, being treated as a serious professional, being trusted. When my tour was over, he asked me to extend. So that was a conversation to have with my wife.
But I had been raised in a CIA that had trained into us that we serve regardless of who sits in the Oval Office, that we are nonpartisan civil servants who will support them with the best information possible. And he was the vice president and needed the best information possible. And so what I would do is I would put that to the side.
It was the fulfillment of what I had always wanted to do, and there were moments like when my tour was finally coming to an end and he invited my family to the White House, and he took my mother’s hand—and this is my mother who had had a really hard time with my transition years before—and Mike Pence took my mother’s hand and says, You must be very proud of your daughter.
And I’m sitting there watching this and I’m thinking, We’ve arrived. There’s no more battles left to be won. I mean, it’s not, that wasn’t true, but it just felt like the two dreams that I’d had since I was a kid, which I had always felt were just completely incompatible.
Harris: You write about the moment that the vice president certified the election and how there was a certain sort of kinship between the two of you around that service, right? That you mentioned the, sort of, bargain, right? The exact quote was, “That was the bargain: service before politics, country before self.”
Can you tell me about that moment? What that moment signified for you?
Curlee: So, this was a few days after January 6 and I had been done briefing him for several months at that point. And he brought us all together, and we were in his West Wing office just down the hall from the Oval, and we went around talking about what serving in this role had meant to us. And I told him that moment, when he had prioritized the country, when he had certified the victory of his opponent in the election, that I was never more proud to have served as his briefer.
And he, you know, he took my hand; we shook hands, and he said that meant a lot to him.
And that is what the bargain meant to me, was the fact that despite our almost certain profound differences of views on many subjects, we could put that aside and treat each other with dignity and do what was right, regardless of our politics and the political cost. And it was a very special moment for me and everybody who was there.
Harris: So, after four years of the Biden administration, the Trump administration comes back for a second time, and people begin to decide whether they should stay or go. So what advice were you getting about what you should do?
Curlee: It was fairly uniform that we should all leave. So during the campaign I had been serving at the White House; I served for about 20 months in the Biden administration as a director for intelligence programs in the NSC. And all throughout that period, it was wall-to-wall TV. I remember standing in the sit room, looking up at one of the many screens and watching these scary images of people like me and hundreds of millions of dollars being poured to create this caricature that somehow trans people were a threat to America and tar the Democratic candidate with association with these scary people. And I’m watching this and in horror that I’m witnessing on the TV the same kind of dehumanization that I’d written PDBs about in my career.
And so, but, despite all of that, despite the warnings from our leadership that they were very afraid for us, that we would be targeted, that it would destroy our careers, that the online mob would be summoned against us—despite all of that, I was the trans woman that briefed Mike Pence. I believed fiercely in the idea of nonpartisan civil service to whoever is the president. And I was not going to walk away from this task that I had been given to help with the peaceful transfer of power of an administration.
And so, the only person in the whole White House, I have to say, who asked us to stay was the president. And I believed it, that was the right decision. And I still believe it still. But almost everyone that decided to do that has paid a price in some form or another.
And so when the politicals departed, about a week out from the turn of administration, I was asked to serve as the acting senior director for intelligence programs. And so I was there when the new team arrived on Inauguration Day. I was there in the West Wing as people were still finding their offices, as people were moving in the furniture and moving in the new furniture, when the vice president arrived and saw his office for the first time. I was there to help the new administration get off the ground. And I did. And for day after day, we did that until the third day, when the administration, while I was briefing the deputy national security adviser, summoned 160 NSE detailees from departments and agencies to a group call and told them they had 15 minutes to get off the compound.
I walked out of my briefing with a handful of taskings that I knew I needed to get to the intelligence community as quickly as possible. And my assistant intercepts me on West Exec, the road between the White House and the EEOB, where my office was, and says, Everyone’s fired except for you. And I was in shock at the recklessness and the callousness of it. And so over the next several days, it was a mess.
And so for the next 69 days, I and the few people from my team that I could bring back served until one day on a Saturday, I’m down in Roanoke, Virginia, with my family, and I get a phone call that says that my tour is over. The chief of staff called. I can’t give you a reason why. You’re gone. You’ll be sent back to CIA. But if you don’t mind, we’d still like you to come in on Monday.
Harris: So you were removed from your position and asked to come back in.
Curlee: Yeah, in the same phone call, you know, fired on Saturday but needed on Monday. But I was warned in that call to be discreet. And I still didn’t understand what was happening until I got off the phone and my iPhone was was bombarded with friend after friend after friend forwarding me a tweet that said, that announced to the world, that there was a trans Biden holdover who hates President Trump in the intelligence directorate, and please give me this person’s name so that I can out them to the world.
And I was terrified of what that would mean for me and my family. But Monday came and I came to work anyway. And I served for another three days to help finish off an important budget item that I had been working on, to turn over a portfolio that I had managed at that point for almost two years, and it was that third night, my last day there, that a list of enemies within the administration was given to the president. And it was yet another purge of people with decades of experience, including my boss at the time.
And, you know, as I was leaving the White House for that last time, with my little box of mementos from two years of serving at the White House, you know, this dream come true, it really hit me what “Be discreet” meant in that point, after everything I had been through with my service to the former vice president, my briefing for this president in the first term, and my war zones, my 20 years, all of it, “Be discreet” meant We need you. We need your service. But we don’t want anyone to know you are here.
And that has stuck with me ever since, and why I have to tell my story, because they’ve taken from me my calling. I can no longer serve. I couldn’t use the bathroom. When I was at the White House, I had to cross the street to coffee shops across Pennsylvania Avenue in order to just get through the day. And the same restrictions followed me back to CIA. And the constant fear of being fired for being who I am just—I couldn’t continue.
But the one thing I can’t allow for me is for the fact that what has happened has already happened. It can’t be undone. And so telling my story is a part of putting that on the record, that someone like me can serve in the White House, can brief a president, can serve honorably, and loves their country.
And so I had to tell this story.
Harris: You mentioned the list of enemies landing on Trump’s desk, and the tweet hunting for the transgender intelligence person in the White House. That tweet and the list came from Laura Loomer, who is a far-right provocateur.
If she never posted that tweet, if that list had never gone out, do you think that you might still be in the White House?
Curlee: I think I probably would have reached my limit at some point in terms of my family, and it would have been time for someone else to come. But I fully intended to keep serving, and at the time it was funny. In that same conversation that I was in with the deputy national security adviser, briefing him on some very sensitive, important programs, he asked me when my tour was over, and I said, Well, sir, it’s been—it’ll be two years and just in a couple months, and, you know, I gotta get home and I’ve got a family. And he said, Hmm, June. I don’t think that’s gonna work for us. And so, I was already starting to think how I was gonna have this conversation again. But I wanted to keep serving, and keep serving at CIA. That was my only plan, and I’m just sad that it became impossible.
Harris: I want to home in on your expertise. You’ve said that what Americans should be concerned about is this wider assault on expertise in this administration, and especially in the intelligence community. So are we already seeing the consequences of that assault on expertise and elimination of expertise?
Curlee: I’m regretting to say we are, and it’s all around us in the evidence of disastrous policies. But to back up a second, you know, the same assault on trans officers, on other minorities, was accompanied by a parallel attack on the ability of our officers to speak truth to power.
So, one of the things that happened early in the new administration was I was asked to send a tasking to the intelligence community on the status of this group Tren de Aragua, which was a Venezuelan street gang. And the tasking was whether the Maduro government had ordered this group to invade the United States, which is the predicate for invoking the Alien Enemies Act almost verbatim, and I tasked it out to the National Intelligence Council, where the chairman of the NIC, which is the most senior analytic body in the intelligence community, dutifully wrote an excellent assessment that reflected the consensus position of the intelligence community. And he and his deputy, when they delivered the product, which did not accord with what the administration wanted to hear, were told that they should rethink their assessment. And when they refused, they were ordered out of the building. And publicly firing one of the most esteemed officers in the intelligence community and their deputy for living up to the values that we inculcate in every young officer was a devastating blow to the whole organization.
And it has had ripple effects all through. And it is just further attacks on officers for assessments that they wrote a decade ago, because they don’t conform with what the president wants to hear, has taught this generation now of officers that your clearance can be revoked with a phone call if you say the wrong thing. And so a muzzle has been put on an organization that is vital to our national interest.
And when you wed that with the destruction of the National Security Council as a policy-coordinating body, which I got to witness firsthand through the purges that unfolded through the first few months of the administration, you’ve lost the very venue in which those concerns and experts and expertise can be delivered to help the president make good decisions. And so it’s not surprising when disastrous outcomes ensue.
So, just for the example, when the country was marching to war in Iran, America launched a full suite of airstrikes showing that the U.S. military is the finest fighting force in the world. And at the same time, the State Department somehow hadn’t planned for the evacuation of half a million Americans and diplomats and officers and their dependents in a war we started.
In any competent administration, regardless of the wisdom of the effort, there would have been a plan. And there would have been a plan to deal with the fact that the Iranians were going to close the Strait of Hormuz. There would have been briefings that would have made clear to the president that decapitating the leadership and killing the supreme leader would not immediately lead to the Iranians surrendering. All of these things are what the intelligence community and the National Security Council should exist to do, to head off these things, to ensure that things that are foreseeable and have been foreseen in multiple public war games for decades about the Iranians would have been delivered and provided context for the administration to make a sound decision or at least plan. And none of it happened.
And as a result, we’re in this debacle where there’s no clear road out, where all the choices are terrible. And we’re looking at ending the conflict in a worse position than when we begun. And there’s, I think there’s a word for that, and it’s called losing a war. And this is a direct result of a climate of fear that the administration has instilled on a workforce that it somehow sees as the enemy within rather than the civil servants who have given their professional lives to helping the country. And we’re all paying for it.
Harris: You wrote that your grandfather told you “Work hard; don’t complain; and the country will take care of you.” Do you still think the country is taking care of you?
Curlee: No, no. It’s hard to feel the sense of betrayal, a bit. And it’s not just me; it’s all of the people who devoted themselves to this ideal of nonpartisan public service, who have been callously thrown away. I’ve got many friends who are transgender in the military, who have faced ruinous financial and life circumstances and had something so important to their identities taken away from them for no reason at all, other than just animus for who some people are.
And that’s why I titled the piece “The Wrong Kind of American,” because it really is that. It is a decision to treat some Americans as not worthy of a full life, of positions of honor, and to treat them as if they’re some sort of threat to society. And it feels as if we’ve just turned our back on the most fundamental ideal that we try to teach everyone, which is that we can rise as far as our talents take us in this country. And that’s a terrible thing.
You know, nine years ago I closed my piece in The Atlantic saying trans kids should know that CIA is always recruiting, because I wanted them to know that there was this amazing life that they could have, that there were some people like them who got to do that, and now I could not in good conscience advise any LGBT American to apply to work at CIA. And that is awful. That is un-American, and I regret saying it, but it’s just true. And I hope that in the coming years that will change and we’ll do what’s right, and we’ll look back at this period in our history with shame and we’ll learn from it.
Harris: Julia, thank you so much for sharing your story and for joining me on the show today.
Curlee: Thank you. It was a privilege.
Harris: That’s all for today’s show.

Verstappen extends Red Bull deal to 2030
- Published
Four-time world champion Max Verstappen has signed a new contract at Red Bull until the end of 2030.
The move should end speculation about the Dutchman's future at the end of this season, after he had been linked with potential moves to Mercedes or McLaren.
Verstappen was previously contracted to the end of 2028, but there were clauses in his contract that would have allowed him to leave at the end of the current Formula 1 season had he wanted.
"We have the best people and I'm excited to keep working together with everyone to get back to the top again," said Verstappen, 28.
"This remains the ultimate goal that all of us have been working towards and will continue to pursue.
"I have always said it: the team is like a second family for me and I feel very at home.
"I came to the team hoping to be able to win races. What we went on to achieve together has been simply lovely and we have shared many incredible moments and won four World Championships.
"To continue this journey with the same team that I have been with my whole career is really special and something I have always wanted to do."
Red Bull have had a difficult start to the era of new regulations for cars and engines introduced for this season.
Verstappen's best results have been two second places, in the Austrian and Hungarian Grands Prix, after coming within two points of beating McLaren's Lando Norris to the world title last season. That 2025 close call followed a dramatic fightback in the second half of the season from a deficit of more than 100 points to the championship lead.
Red Bull's lack of performance has led to Verstappen voicing frustration on a number of occasions, but in the end he has decided to stick with what he knows.
The decision comes despite his trusted race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase signing to join McLaren by 2028.
Verstappen's renewal statement included praise for team principal Laurent Mekies, who took over last July after former boss Christian Horner was sacked following a turbulent 18-month period and a decline in competitiveness.
"Getting to work with Laurent now for over a year has also been great, I see a clear vision he has for the team," Verstappen said.
"Everyone [at Red Bull's base] in Milton Keynes believes in what we are building and I am looking forward to the next chapter, fighting for more victories and competing for championships as we continue to shape the future of this team."
The announcement has been timed to coincide with Verstappen's final home race this weekend before the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort falls off the calendar.
Although the deal takes Verstappen to the end of 2030, there are still mechanisms by which he could leave if performance does not come up to expectations.
This is standard practice in driver contracts in F1. The details are not yet known, and teams do not comment on contractual intricacies.
Mekies said: "Having Max continue with us and retaining the best driver on the grid is fantastic news.
"Very few partnerships in sport achieve what Max and this team have. Since the very beginning, Max has embodied everything that makes Red Bull Racing special: uncompromising competitiveness, relentless determination and the courage to challenge convention.
"His impact on our team and Red Bull's motorsport story has been transformational and he has been fundamental to everything we have achieved together.
"The decision to continue our journey together is rooted in the trust Max and the team have built over many years, as well as Max's confidence in our people, our culture and our vision for the future.
"Forged through championship-winning success, intense battles and challenging moments alike, this relationship has only grown stronger – making it one of Formula 1's greatest success stories. But we are not done yet. There are more races to win, more milestones to achieve and more history to write."
Verstappen started his F1 career with Red Bull's junior team, then called Toro Rosso, in 2015. He was promoted to the senior team after four races of his second season, 2016, and immediately won his first race.
He has since gone on to win 71 grands prix alongside his four world titles, with his tally of race victories ranking third in all-time F1 history after Lewis Hamilton and Michael Schumacher.

During the #MeToo movement in India, around 2018, there were few articles in the press written by Indian men that engaged seriously with what women were saying about sexual violence and with the social conditions that allow it to persist. But instead of a failure of individual men to support women, the gap reflected a difficulty in thinking about gender-based violence as something produced by individual acts as well as by social relationships and assumptions about masculinity.
By and large, men’s responses then, as now, following the Bombay High Court’s commendable decision to reverse Tarun Tejpal’s acquittal, have instinctively been to become defensive or huddle together rather than open up, meet women on their terms, and think through and talk about sexual violence.
What we can say
On August 11, a senior Supreme Court advocate argued in The Tribune that because criminal law can punish only conduct that satisfies the legal requirements of an existing offence, we should suspend judgment on the Tejpal case and wait for the decision of the Supreme Court, where Mr. Tejpal has appealed. A court cannot convict someone for conduct that does not constitute an offence under the law — and due process and the presumption of innocence are legitimate subjects of discussion. However, it does not follow that the only appropriate response outside the courtroom, as the advocate says, is to say “we do not know”. We can still distinguish between what a criminal court is legally entitled to conclude and what the social dimensions of a case allows society to conclude.
In 2022, Andrea Waling, honorary adjunct at the Australian Research Centre in Sex, Health and Society, Melbourne, reported in a paper in the Journal of Men’s Studies “five key framings” in #MeToo coverage based on 163 media reports: “men are victims of masculinity requiring intervention, men are positioned as inherently ‘good’ or ‘bad’, boys and men are lost and need to be found, men are performative in their ‘awakenings’, and men’s take up of protector or allyship roles may in fact be attempts to be false heroes”.
“The findings of this work note several tensions and contradictions that highlight an overall lack of coherency and agreement regarding men’s engagements with, and roles in, the #MeToo movement,” she added.
Misleading distinction
The fact is, men saying “I support women” is not the same as men asking uncomfortable questions about masculinity, desire, entitlement, friendship, professional hierarchies, male conversations, complicity, and the ways ordinary men may participate in cultures that make sexual violence possible without themselves being predators per se. This is also the territory the #MeToo movement opened up in India but which men have seemed the least willing to enter. In an article in The Indian Express in 2018, Rimjhim Jain wrote that men were the “missing piece” of India’s #MeToo movement and that their silence has allowed the problem to continue to be framed as something women themselves have to resolve. That has not changed.
Men have remarkably little practice talking about sexual violence as a male problem. Instead, there is copious male discourse about false accusations, due process, the presumption of innocence, men being afraid to interact with women, and so on. Laws also reflect the society that makes them and criminal cases cannot encompass conduct the law already does not criminalise. However, none of this means other questions are illegitimate, or even less important. In particular, men still need to ask what it is about the specific social organisation of relations between men and women that produces the situations the law eventually confronts.
That in turn requires us to move beyond the misleading distinction between “men like us” and “other men” and to recognise that sexual violence is not the preserve of ‘monsters’. It can also emerge from ordinary assumptions about, say, flirting, persistence, seniority, alcohol, women’s accommodation of male behaviour, and men being disinclined to intervene when another man crosses a line. This is also why a group response by men can become a form of mutual psychological protection: “Let us establish that we are not all monsters,” they seem to say, “before we discuss what the group itself has to examine”.
Sexual violence cannot be understood using abstract political analysis alone. Instead, it demands attention to intimate behaviour. Put another way, it is not enough to identify The System as being patriarchal; at some point you have to ask how you should behave. How the men around you behave. What you have laughed at. What you have ignored. And whom you have believed — or not. A criminal trial has to determine whether particular conduct satisfies a particular legal standard but society can, and should, also ask what kinds of behaviour it ought to have learned to recognise as unacceptable before they reached the threshold of criminal proceedings.
Original insight
Fixating on the intellectual objects on the basis of which the High Court reversed the lower court’s decision in the Tejpal case, such as evidence, testimonies, criminal laws, standards of proof, judicial reasoning, and so on, also allows men a way to avoid confronting the larger question #MeToo posed. That is: what forms of sexual coercion, intimidation, and entitlement exist in the gap between behaviour that is socially acceptable and conduct that a criminal court can recognise and punish? As at the height of the #MeToo years, this question remains relevant, and in India still barely charted.
In fact, that the legal system reached different conclusions at different times validates #MeToo’s original insight, that there is a distinction between what a criminal court can establish in an individual case and what a society needs to learn to identify and change.
Women have exercised much of the intellectual labour of making this subject discussable whereas men have often treated it as something to consume rather than participate in. Today there are also sophisticated feminist analyses of consent, coercion, power, institutional complicity, testimonial injustice, workplace hierarchy, etc. One would like to see a corresponding body of male self-reflection asking what it would mean for men to understand themselves — ourselves — differently.

I left my wife and twins behind - why this Nigerian man fled South Africa
- Published
Nigerian Richard Itoro is not sure when he will see his twin children again.
Fearing for his safety as the anti-migrant protests cranked up in South Africa this year, the 47-year-old left his family and business behind in Johannesburg and boarded one of the voluntary repatriation flights to Nigeria in June.
His is just one of many experiences that is fuelling diplomatic tension and threatening to rupture relations between South Africa and other countries on the continent.
Tens of thousands of foreigners have left the country over the past two months.
"It was painful for me to leave [the] person who's my best friend," Itoro tells the BBC, with tears welling up, as he reflects on saying goodbye to his South African wife.
Over 15 years, he had built up a car-dealership business, bought a home and created a family. That is now all gone for him.
Itoro became the target of harassment but his wife was not spared the intimidation.
He says his neighbours told her: "You're married to a Nigerian. Those of you who are married to Nigerians we are supposed to arrest you people.
"You guys betrayed us. Go and leave the country with your husband and don't be here."
Itoro was baffled.
"My family was just a small family, which was beautiful and peaceful. I had no issues with anybody."
The pressure became too much.
"If I go home and start all over again, it's better than being here, being harassed, being scared for my life," Itoro says.
But, the businessman says, the Nigerian high commission would not let his wife and children travel with him.
He describes how leaving felt like a movie where someone boards the last helicopter flight out of a besieged city.
"I wish I could have just begged the people from the embassy and said: 'This is my wife, I can't leave her behind and my kids,' but I couldn't.
"So my car started departing and I wished I had told her not to cry."
The anti-migrant groups in South Africa said their protests were aimed at undocumented foreigners. The country's outspoken Culture Minister, Gayton McKenzie, who leads one of the parties in the coalition government, also emphasised this point.
"We say South Africa is open to our brothers on the continent but come here legitimately. Come with your papers," he told the BBC's Interview programme.
But Itoro says his legal status did not protect him from hostility as he shows the BBC a copy of the document that he says proves he had the right to stay in the country.
He was not alone, according to the Nigerian authorities.
"We have records of Nigerians who have legitimate papers to remain in South Africa, yet they have been attacked," Nigeria's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Sola Enikanolaiye said during a recent meeting with South Africa's Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.
The temperature was raised last week following the death of a Nigerian who was killed as police were arresting him over suspected drug offences. An independent body is now investigating.
Lamola maintained that South Africa deals with those who take the law into their own hands, but added that President Cyril Ramaphosa was also "very firm on South Africa's sovereign right to enforce its immigration laws".
Despite the diplomatic efforts, South Africa's reputation has been severely damaged.
Not least because of images and videos circulating on social media. Not all of them were what they were purported to be, but one, involving a Ghanaian, was genuine and it sparked huge concern once it started being shared in April.
When Emmanuel Asamoah left Ghana in 2023 for South Africa, he was chasing the kind of opportunity many migrants dream about.
The 37-year-old hairstylist settled in Soweto, on the outskirts of Johannesburg, found work, built a life and believed he had a future in one of Africa's biggest economies.
But three months ago that future suddenly felt uncertain when he was surrounded by a group of South Africans who demanded that he leave. The confrontation was captured on video.
"This thing of you guys moving from one country to another… is no longer working," one woman can be seen telling Asamoah.
"Now, we are making it very clear to you guys, we don't want you here. We want you to fix your countries."
Having returned to Ghana's capital, Accra, in May, Asamoah tells the BBC that the encounter left him terrified.
"They came to me and started pushing me... So, they started asking questions and harassing me… they said that I should go home, that we are spoiling their country, because of us, they don't eat, we are taking their girlfriends," he says.
South Africa's high jobless rate - standing at more than 30% - is seen as one of the factors fuelling the tension. It was a sentiment echoed by McKenzie.
"No man can feed another man's children while his children are starving. Our people are starving of jobs," he said backing calls for those who came to the country without papers to leave.
But Asamoah insists he had a stamp in his passport giving him permission to stay.
"I was not illegal. I was legal in South Africa. That's why I told them that, they can take me to the police station so that we can go to Home Affairs and verify," he says.
For Asamoah, returning home has brought an unexpected fresh start.
With support from a Ghanaian businessman, he has opened a cement business and is determined to build his future.
"My brothers and sisters in South Africa. I'm in Ghana now. I'm fixing my country," he says.
But Ghana's government remains angry at the way it sees its citizens are being viewed in South Africa.
In an interview with the BBC, Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa spoke about how he saw it as going against the spirit of continental solidarity and a failure to recognise how African countries helped in the struggle against apartheid, which ended in 1994.
South Africa "should be the epitome of Pan-Africanism. We talk about African integration. We talk about free movement… even if you have issues with high immigration, is this how you resolve it?", the minister asked.
In Lagos, Itoro is still pining for his family.
"It's not easy. But we talk every day, and I'm broken. There is hope, because... my wife is going to join me very soon, as soon as God lifts me up. But it was heartbreaking, and that's how I felt: like I lost everything," he says.

Why everyone is talking about Trump's aide Natalie Harp
U.S. president's assistant under media scrutiny is known for extreme devotion to Trump
When U.S. President Donald Trump used a catering truck to secretly move from Air Force One during a potential security threat in Turkey early last month, a number of people remained on the plane.
They included U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the 13-person press pool.
Among those who made the move with Trump: deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino, director of Oval Office operations Walt Nauta and the woman who is suddenly in the middle of a U.S. media firestorm: executive assistant Natalie Harp.
Who is Natalie Harp?
The 35-year-old is special assistant and executive assistant to the president. She can often be seen by his side both in the Oval Office and when he travels. She went to court with him when he was facing trials and was at both 2024 assassination attempts.
Fox News said in a profile shortly after Trump won his second term that Harp has been alongside the president since 2022.
"I believe she is an extra set of eyes and ears for President Trump," Sen. John Barrasso, a Republican from Wyoming, told Fox News then. "Every time I have been with him, she has been close at hand." He added: "If he doesn't pick up the phone, I know to go to Natalie, and he gets the message."
Harp has set up a mobile office that travels with Trump, including a mobile printer to get articles in front of him immediately when needed.
She first became part of Trump's world in 2019, after the bone cancer survivor lauded the president for a 2018 law meant to give patients access to experimental treatments before approval.
Multiple Republicans have stressed her loyalty to the president, and she speaks of him in glowing terms.
In the Fox profile, she said: "He is on a totally different plane, at peace with God and unshakably focused. Nothing gets to him, because he puts his comfort second and his purpose first."
New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, in their book Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump, said Harp alarmed the U.S. Secret Service during the election campaign by leaving Trump adoring letters in his private quarters, including one that said, "You are all that matters to me."
Why is she in the news now?
Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff.
The Georgia senator is running for re-election and has been floated as a presidential candidate, though he denies any interest in the campaign for 2028.
At a campaign event on Sunday, Ossoff said that Trump doesn't want to do the job.
"He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenceless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar," he said, referring in turn to White House renovations, Harp and Air Force One.
Trump's response
On Monday, a reporter in the Oval Office asked Trump about Ossoff's comments.
"You mean Pee-wee Herman?" Trump said. "Pee-wee Herman look-alike. No, I would much rather do other things. It's a — we're building a great facility here. We're fixing a White House that hasn't been taken care of."
White House communications director Steven Cheung used vulgar terms to describe Ossoff and said he was the biggest "loser" in politics. Conservative commentators accused Ossoff of sexism and, given Harp's cancer history, heartlessness.
Democrats and other people opposed to Trump have been giddy about Ossoff's comments, or at least willing to play along. "Ok I'll bite," Michigan state Senate majority whip Mallory McMorrow wrote on X. "Who's Natalie."
The Pod Save America podcast, which is hosted by former Obama speechwriters and aides, said it was mission accomplished for Ossoff because his comments went viral online and made news while winking at rumours there is more than a presidential-staffer relationship. (There is no evidence of any improper relationship.)
"I think there's a question of whether it might kick up media coverage of these allegations now in a way that is frustrating to the White House," said co-host Tommy Vietor.

India is facing a critical nationwide shortage of two key chemotherapy drugs, cisplatin and carboplatin, driven by soaring global platinum raw material costs, West Asia shipping route disruptions, and domestic price caps. While government hospitals in several States have managed to stabilise supplies, private hospitals in many parts are still facing a crunch. For patients, this has meant interruptions or delays in life-saving treatment. In response, the government last month raised temporarily ceiling rates for the two drugs by 50%, to help restart halted domestic manufacturing lines.
What’s happening?
Cisplatin is a chemotherapeutic agent used in the treatment of solid tumors as well as certain blood cancers. Carboplatin is a second generation platinum compound that is also used to treat solid tumours. Both are among the most widely used chemotherapy drugs in India and are indispensable in the treatment of several cancers, including ovarian, head and neck, lung, gall bladder, urinary bladder, breast and testicular cancers.
Prices for platinum—the core raw material used in cisplatin and carboplatin—more than doubled, making old price-controlled manufacturing rates financially unviable for companies. Additionally, geopolitical conflicts and shipping constraints through West Asia have restricted raw material imports from primary global suppliers. This resulted in several generic makers temporarily slowing or stopping production of these drugs, says Sayoni Bhanja, consultant, medical oncology at HCG Cancer Centre, Kolkata.
Impact on hospitals, patients
At the Cancer Institute (WIA), Adyar, in Chennai, Kalpana Balakrishnan, chief executive officer and medical director, said that the shortage has been ongoing for nearly seven months due to the war and has had significant impacts. “The cheapest drug, cisplatin, a first-generation platinum drug, is not available. Carboplatin and oxaliplatin, which are second and third generation platinum drugs, are considerably more expensive.”
Sujith Kumar Mullapally, senior consultant - medical oncology, Apollo Proton Cancer Centre, Chennai said that the hospital has not received cisplatin and carboplatin from its regular companies for a long time now and was depending on companies which are Indian generic companies. He added that they have managed up until now with available stocks, and that through medical oncology forums, significant efforts have been made to inform the necessary authorities.
In Karnataka, some hospitals reported stocks sufficient for only six to eight weeks.
Amit Rauthan, head of medical oncology, immunotherapy and precision medicine at Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, Bengaluru, said cisplatin and carboplatin are also critical in treating childhood cancers such as neuroblastoma, hepatoblastoma, germ cell tumours and retinoblastoma, and that their therapeutic role cannot be easily replaced by alternative medicines.
Vijay Kumar Srinivasalu, senior consultant in medical oncology at Sakra World Hospital, Bengaluru, said platinum-based chemotherapy continues to be the backbone of treatment for several solid tumours despite advances in targeted therapies and immunotherapy. Treatment delays or substitution with less effective regimens could compromise outcomes, particularly in curative-intent cancers. This is especially significant in concurrent chemoradiation for cervical and head and neck cancers, where weekly cisplatin plays a vital role in enhancing the effectiveness of radiation therapy, he noted.
For patients, this has meant delays and interruptions in treatment, additional stress, as well as increased costs.
The immediate fallout, said, Sandeep Nayak, chairman of oncology, MACS-Renova Oncology Institute, KIMS Hospital, Bengaluru lands directly on cancer patients: while alternative treatment regimens exist, they are generally less effective, non-standard, and can carry higher costs or different toxicity profiles.
The disruptions are leading to treatment delays, changes in chemotherapy regimens and additional financial and psychological stress for patients and their families, warned Smitha Saldanha, consultant in medical oncology at HCG Cancer Hospital, K.R. Road, Bengaluru.
Bhawna Sirohi, medical oncologist and medical director of Vedanta Medical Research Foundation, Raipur, Chhattisgarh, said for patients this may mean a compromise on curative cancer treatment.
How the government sector is faring
The government sector seems to be doing better in several States.
At the Regional Cancer Centre, Kerala in Thiruvananthapuram, treatment was not disrupted as the hospital had adequate stock of platinum-based drugs to tide over a few months, said director, R Rejnishkumar. “We were beginning to get worried too, as we could not get any response for the purchase tenders we floated. But now that the government has revised the prices, our purchase process is going forward and I am told that we will get new stock soon,” Dr. Rejnish said.
The Karnataka government-run Kidwai Memorial Institute of Oncology in Bengaluru has said it currently has adequate stocks and multiple procurement channels to ensure continuity of care. “We have annual tenders in place and procure medicines through the Central Medical Store as well as the Kidwai Cancer Drug Foundation (KCDF). We also have multiple vendors, and non-governmental organisations support us by supplying these drugs,” said KMIO director (in charge), R. Krishnappa.
At the Delhi State Cancer Institute, both cisplatin and carboplatin injections are currently available and chemotherapy services are continuing as per clinical schedules, said Pragya Shukla, head of clinical oncology.
Sources in the T.N. government said that cisplatin was in the essential drugs list of the Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation and hence, its supply was ensured. However, carboplatin, a speciality drug, was unavailable for bulk purchases but hospitals were managing through local purchases.
In Telangana, however, the Mehdi Nawaz Jung Institute of Oncology and Regional Cancer Centre in Hyderabad, the State’s largest and only government tertiary cancer care hospital, has been grappling with a shortage of both cisplatin and carboplatin for the past two months, with supplies falling well short of its monthly requirement. Sadashivudu Gundeti, Director of MNJ Institute of Oncology, said the institute requires thousands of vials of the two chemotherapy drugs every month but is currently able to procure only a few hundred vials. Suppliers have informed the hospital that they were currently unable to meet its full requirement, he said. He expressed hope that supplies could become adequate by the end of August.
What the government has done
On June 12, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) invoked special clauses to raise the price cap of cisplatin from ₹7.26 to ₹10.89 per mL, and carboplatin from ₹60.49 rupees to ₹90.74 per mL, citing public interest. The increase is a one-time revision and will be reviewed after six months, the NPPA said. India is heavily dependent on imported platinum, and the measure was aimed at boosting domestic manufacture to restock depleted supply chains.
Boben Thomas, a consultant medical and paediatric oncologist in Thiruvananthapuram said companies have now resumed manufacturing these drugs. However, doctors have pointed out that short-term measures are not a permanent solution.
Long-term strategies
With more than 1.5 million new cancer cases diagnosed annually in India, Dr. Saldanha said uninterrupted access to essential oncology medicines must be treated as a national healthcare priority.
While describing the recent revision of ceiling prices as a useful short-term measure, Dr. Srinivasalu said India requires a long-term oncology drug security framework, including strategic reserves of essential cancer medicines, diversified domestic manufacturing, stronger active pharmaceutical ingredient supply chains, centralised procurement and an early-warning system for anticipated shortages.
Dr. Saldanha called for coordinated action involving manufacturers, regulators, healthcare providers and policymakers to strengthen domestic production, build strategic buffer stocks and ensure equitable distribution of essential chemotherapy drugs across the country.
A Union Health Ministry official said the Central government has taken all steps to ensure that the supply chain stays stable. In case any State or patient faces any issue regarding availability or access to the drug, they may approach the concerned department, the official said.
(With inputs from Afshan Yasmeen in Bengaluru, Shrabana Chatterjee in Kolkata, Serena Josephine M. in Chennai, C. Maya in Thiruvananthapuram, Bindu Shajan Perappadan in Delhi and Siddharth Kumar Singh in Hyderabad.)

There’s No Reason to Buy a New Phone Anymore
Consumers are ditching the hype cycle and buying used devices in unprecedented numbers.
In a time when an iPhone can be preordered, customized, and on its way to your doorstep all through a touch-screen tap, it’s almost quaint to remember that people used to camp out for smartphone releases. That was once the regular routine of Andrew Erickson, a longtime tech YouTuber, who recalled to me with a mixture of nostalgia and awe the time he braved the rain at 4:30 a.m. to join a line for the newest iPhone. The line snaked through the mall, nearly reaching the parking lot.
Next month, when Apple is expected to launch the iPhone 18 Pro, Erickson has no plans to even buy the phone, let alone fight crowds for it. Instead, along with a growing number of Americans, Erickson is buying used. He’s fed up with incremental improvements in gadgets, he told me, and is more interested in getting an old version of the iPhone 17 Pro when it hits the secondhand market at a discount. Already, almost half of his current devices were acquired secondhand, and as electronics prices soar amid an AI-fueled chip shortage, he expects that portion to grow. “The argument’s just getting weaker and weaker to buy brand-new,” he said.
Based on the numbers, old tech products are indeed being looked at in a new light. Globally, the size of the industry could reach $153.4 billion this year, up from $104.1 billion four years ago. The used-smartphone market alone is expected to grow by more than 12 percent in 2026, according to the International Data Corporation, which forecasts that the market for new smartphones will experience a record drop this year. Growth in secondhand electronics and refurbished gadgets that have been restored to full working condition now outpaces that of new products on eBay, the e-commerce giant reports.
Among a number of shoppers I spoke with, there was a sense that new models are indistinguishable from the old ones, and the hype of securing the latest and greatest has given way to an upgrade cycle driven by practicality. More than ever before, people are eager to buy used.
“We’ve never been here,” Lauren Benton, the U.S. general manager of the refurbished-electronics marketplace Back Market, told me. She said demand ticked up immediately after Apple unveiled price hikes this summer. Back Market’s order values for refurbished MacBooks in the U.S. increased by 37 percent throughout the week following the price increase, while order values for iPads rose 25 percent. Demand for the company’s non-Apple laptops, too, has soared by 74 percent compared with last year. Outside of students and parents, a large portion of the marketplace’s buyers are “people that understand that the newer tech isn’t giving us all that much more,” Benton said.
Regular upgrade cycles were a hallmark of tech gadgets in the 2010s, a trend led by Apple, which has introduced at least one new iPhone model every year since its initial launch. Americans bought into the frenzy: In 2014, the first year Consumer Intelligence Research Partners tracked such figures, about 44 percent of iPhone holders said they replaced their device every one to two years. In those days, lines at Apple stores stretched so long that they were used by analysts to gauge annual demand.
In 2026, the lines that former Apple fanatics once waited in have all but disappeared. Online preorders are partly to blame, but so is dissipating excitement for releases that promise incremental upgrades. People now hold on to their smartphone for three years or longer, fatigued from “buying, effectively, the same device over and over and over again,” Wamsi Mohan, a Bank of America analyst who covers Apple, told me. Those buying new are doing so largely because their phone was broken or stolen, rather than to get their hands on new features. A recent report found that 76 percent of buyers refuse to upgrade until new capabilities feel “worth the cost.”
And those costs are climbing, driven by data centers eating up the world’s inventory of RAM. Samsung’s Galaxy Tab S11, Sony’s PlayStation 5, and Microsoft’s XBox Series S console were all marked up $100 this year. Apple conceded to “unavoidable” hikes in June, increasing the cost of its MacBooks and iPads by roughly 15 to 25 percent. Even the most ardent tech loyalists have changed their buying habits: A recent poll of thousands of readers of 9to5Mac, a website popular among Apple fans, revealed that 38 percent of them intended to upgrade less frequently because of higher prices.
In tandem, people are warming up to refurbished devices. Google queries for secondhand laptop have jumped by upwards of 5,000 percent over the past year. In an April CNET survey, nearly half of U.S. adults said they’d considered buying refurbished tech within the past year and cited cost-effectiveness and expensive new models as driving factors. Angie Cardona-Nelson, who recycles used electronics on eBay, told me that when she started her business in 2008, selling refurbished devices was tough going—she’d sit on products for months, attempting to drum up business with sales or discounts. “There was no confidence to buy a used item,” she said. Since January 2025, her laptop sales have more than doubled, and new listings are being bought up in a week or two.
The way people are buying secondhand devices has also shifted: Instead of opting for products that are roughly three generations behind, buyers are purchasing last year’s models—an indication that the refurbished industry is now attracting those who were “truly considering new,” according to Back Market’s Benton.
Erik Helgesen, the president of PayMore, a retail chain focused on used electronics, told me that the company had already seen a major uptick in sales preceding Apple’s price hike. But after, it was “just a hockey stick,” he said. Now PayMore can hardly keep some products in stock. Helgesen expects the company to open more stores in the coming year to meet demand.
This new readiness to opt out of the endless treadmill of releases seems to be a sign that people are starting to look for something more practical from their devices: deals. Whether this more utilitarian—and arguably healthier—approach to gadget consumption means that we’ll actually free ourselves from expensive tech, though, remains to be seen. A three-year-old MacBook may be a steal today, but as Nabila Popal, a senior director at the International Data Corporation, reminded me, prices reflect demand: If people keep buying up the used gadgets, those prices are bound to shoot up, too.

Brown went aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln for several days starting in early July, as confirmed by the Department of Defense, Brown and videos of her broadcasts from the ship. Following reports in August of deteriorating conditions aboard the Lincoln in August, Brown summarized her experience on the Lincoln as "something messier than a single narrative" where sailors reported "genuine hardship alongside genuine resilience."
In August 2026, national attention turned to the USS Abraham Lincoln, the aircraft carrier deployed to the waters around Iran since January, after reporting came out about deteriorating conditions and concerns about sailors' mental health as the ship's deployment continued to drag on. Following the reports, the U.S. Department of Defense sent the USS George Washington to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln and relieve it from duty.
As the reports emerged, critics of President Donald Trump's administration highlighted the conditions the sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln reportedly suffered as a result of the aircraft carrier's long deployment. As part of a desire to bring more attention to these reports, some social media posts praised CNN's Pamela Brown for allegedly visiting the vessel and telling "the truth Trump doesn't want you to hear," as one Facebook post (archived) described it.
According to the post, what Brown found on the USS Abraham Lincoln "was more human and more damning than any single headline." The post read:
Sailors dealing with black mold, food so bad that crew members were losing weight, and no idea when they were going home. The ship has been deployed for nearly nine months. Multiple sailors have attempted to jump overboard. And the number one issue crushing morale wasn't the mold or the food. It was the silence. No end date. No clarity. No honesty from the people who sent them there.One sailor put it plainly in a message to Brown. What started as a two-week combat operation became seven months with a shifting justification every few weeks. First it was to help Iranian protesters. Then to denuclearize Iran. Then to support a blockade. Nobody could tell them why they were still there or when they were coming home, while their families had their lives on hold waiting for them.Hegseth called coverage of the Lincoln "completely misrepresented." Brown wrote that sentiment "did not go over well" with the sailors she's been talking to. That is as politely as a journalist can call a defense secretary a liar.Thank you, Pamela Brown, for getting on that ship and letting those sailors be heard.
(Facebook)
Similar claims about Brown going on board the USS Abraham Lincoln also appeared on Instagram (archived) and Threads (archived), and Snopes readers searched our site for information about whether she really visited the aircraft carrier.
The claim that Brown went aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln and reported on sailors' conditions from the ship is true — a
Brown's own account of the conditions aboard the Lincoln during her time on it was also more nuanced than the social media posts suggested, and she did not paint an entirely negative picture.
Confirming Brown's time aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln
According to an article by Brown that CNN published in August about her time on the USS Abraham Lincoln, she boarded the aircraft carrier on July 7. On July 9, she reported live from on board the ship on a CNN broadcast. By July 13, video available on CNN's website shows she was back in the studio at CNN reporting about her experience on the Lincoln.
In that segment, Brown talked about how the sailors said they went months without fresh fruit and vegetables during a time when rations were low
While on board the Lincoln in July, Brown 
In August, the Department of Defense confirmed over X (archived) Brown was on the Lincoln "last month." In an apparent attempt to refute reports of deteriorating conditions aboard the aircraft carrier, the Defense Department highlighted (archived) that Brown and her crew ate ice cream while on the ship.
Immediately after her return from the Lincoln, CNN ran a segment of Brown's interviews with sailors highlighting the mental toll the long deployment had on the ship's crew, as well as what the ship's leadership was doing to support their mental health.
Brown wrote about these experiences in her written account of her time on the Lincoln in August. That account was the same one referenced in the above social media posts.
What Brown wrote about her time aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln
According to Brown, sailors described losing "significant weight" because meals at one point were "reduced to tuna mixed with noodles, or corn dogs." By the time she arrived, she wrote in the August CNN article, food was plentiful and there were morale-boosting events like ice cream socials, but sailors still had to wait in line for up to an hour for each meal.
Brown wrote that she didn't personally notice widespread black mold, but a sailor aboard the ship had messaged her that there had been "black mold around the ship for awhile."
Some sailors told Brown of low morale, while others said it felt better than past deployments simply because it had Wi-Fi. Others spoke of camaraderie between the ship's crew, Brown wrote.
The hardest part for sailors, Brown wrote, was the open-ended extension of the ship's deployment.
